- [Google Cloud: Health checks overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/health-check-concepts)
02.07:
Consistent-hashing load balancing routes a key to a backend so that the same key tends to reach the same place, while adding or removing a backend moves only part of the key space. It is useful for cache locality and some partitioned state. It is not automatically the best way to spread ordinary stateless requests.

## Why ordinary modulo is disruptive

Suppose a cache has four nodes and assigns a product with `hash(product_id) mod 4`. Adding a fifth node changes the divisor. Many product keys map to different nodes, causing a broad cache miss storm even though the underlying catalog did not change. A consistent-hash scheme maps both keys and nodes into a common hash space and assigns each key to a nearby node. When a node joins, it takes over a portion of neighboring keys rather than remapping almost everything.

Karger and collaborators introduced the idea for distributed web caching. The precise movement depends on the scheme and balance, but the useful property is stability as membership changes. Implementations often use multiple virtual positions per physical node to smooth uneven ranges. More virtual positions improve balance at the cost of a larger routing table and more movement bookkeeping.

| Routing method | Membership change | Typical fit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Round robin | No key affinity | Stateless request replicas |
| `hash(key) mod N` | Broad remapping when `N` changes | Fixed small shard count |
| Consistent hash ring | Limited key movement | Cache or partition locality |
| Rendezvous hashing | Limited movement without ring traversal | Key-to-node assignment |

## Choose a stable key

The routing key must correspond to the state you want to keep local. Hashing a client IP can put unrelated users behind one NAT on the same backend and send one user's requests to different backends as their network changes. Hashing a session ID or cache key may better reflect locality. The key must be available at the load balancer and should have high enough cardinality to distribute work.

Hot keys remain a problem. If one celebrity account receives half the traffic, every request for that key can land on one node, even if the hash space is otherwise balanced. Replication, key splitting, or an application-level hot-key strategy may be necessary. Consistent hashing balances *keys* probabilistically; it does not guarantee balanced work when key popularity is skewed.

## Handle membership and failure explicitly

All routers must agree on the active node set and hash function. If two gateways have different membership views, the same key may reach different backends during a transition. That can be acceptable for a disposable cache but dangerous for state that requires one writer. For durable shards, define rebalancing, data migration, ownership handoff, and how writes behave during a node failure. A routing algorithm alone does not move bytes or prevent split-brain writes.

In a cache, a failed node's keys move to successors and miss until warmed. Plan for that temporary backend load. In a sticky application session, a failed node may lose local state; consistent routing does not make it durable. NGINX exposes a `hash ... consistent` upstream mode, but its presence should not be mistaken for a complete data-partition protocol.

## Design review

What exact key is hashed, and why does it represent useful locality? What fraction of work moves on a node addition or failure? Are key sizes and request rates evenly distributed? Who moves or reconstructs state when ownership changes?

## Sources

- [Karger et al.: Consistent Hashing and Random Trees](https://people.csail.mit.edu/karger/Papers/web.pdf)
- [NGINX: `hash` upstream directive](https://nginx.org/en/docs/http/ngx_http_upstream_module.html#hash)
02.08:
An event contract tells consumers what happened, how to identify that occurrence, and how to interpret its data. A topic name and an arbitrary JSON blob are insufficient when several independently deployed services depend on the event. The contract includes semantics, envelope fields, payload schema, ordering, delivery expectations, and evolution rules.

## Name a fact that has already occurred

An event such as `OrderPlaced` should mean the order reached a defined durable state. If it can later be rejected by payment, perhaps `OrderSubmitted` is more honest. Consumers may take irreversible actions based on the name, so distinguish a fact from a command or tentative workflow step. The producer owns the meaning and should publish only after the underlying state transition is committed.

A useful envelope includes an event ID, source, type, occurrence time, schema version or reference, and trace or correlation ID. The payload carries domain facts such as order ID, customer ID, currency, and total. CloudEvents standardizes several envelope attributes, including `id`, `source`, `type`, and `specversion`; the `source` plus `id` combination identifies a distinct event. Your product still defines what `OrderPlaced` means and what its fields mean.

| Field | Purpose | Example question |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Event ID | Deduplication and tracing | Is it stable across delivery retries? |
| Entity ID | Associate related events | Can consumers key state by order? |
| Occurred time | Business timeline | Is it source time or broker time? |
| Schema version | Decode payload | How are old versions retained? |
| Correlation ID | Follow a workflow | Which request caused the event? |

## Define delivery and ordering

Many brokers can redeliver after a consumer crash. Treat consumers as at-least-once unless the entire end-to-end contract proves otherwise. A consumer should store a processed-event ID or make its side effect naturally idempotent. Ordering may exist only within a partition keyed by entity ID. If order events are keyed differently, `OrderCancelled` could be observed before `OrderPlaced` by one consumer. State the ordering scope and how consumers handle gaps or replays.

Payloads should contain enough facts for the intended consumers without exposing unnecessary private data. If a consumer needs a current snapshot, a small event with only an ID forces a synchronous fetch and reintroduces coupling. If the event copies every internal field, it becomes a privacy and compatibility burden. Choose the event's public facts deliberately and document who may subscribe.

## Evolve schemas without breaking consumers

Adding an optional field is usually easier than removing a required one. A new enum value may still surprise a consumer. Establish compatibility rules and test old consumers against new producer examples. For a breaking semantic change, publish a new event type or version, run both during migration, then retire the old form after consumer adoption is measured. Avoid silently changing the unit of an existing field, such as cents to dollars.

Keep example events in the contract and validate them in CI. Include duplicate, missing optional field, old schema, and out-of-order cases in consumer tests. When a producer changes, check not only that JSON parses but also that the event is emitted at the same point in the business workflow.

## Design review

What exact committed fact does this event assert? Can a consumer deduplicate it after a crash? Which events are ordered relative to it? Can a consumer using last month's schema still understand the new payload?

## Sources

- [CloudEvents specification](https://github.com/cloudevents/spec/blob/main/cloudevents/spec.md)
- [Microsoft Azure Architecture Center: Event-driven architecture](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/architecture-styles/event-driven)
02.09:
Timeouts bound how long a caller waits. Retries give a transient failure another chance. Idempotency makes repeating an operation safe when the caller cannot tell whether the previous attempt succeeded. These mechanisms must be designed together; adding retries alone can multiply load and duplicate side effects.

## Start with the ambiguous outcome

A client sends `POST /payments` and the connection times out. The server may have charged the card and lost the response, or it may have failed before charging. A blind retry with a new operation ID risks a second charge. The client sends a stable idempotency key for the intended payment, and the server stores the key with the result or durable operation state. A retry with the same key returns the same logical result, subject to a documented retention window and parameter-mismatch policy.

Not every request should be retried. A validation error is permanent until input changes. A short network failure or `503` may be transient. A `429` can indicate a rate limit and may include guidance about when to retry. Retry behavior belongs in the API contract, especially for writes whose side effects matter. AWS's Builders' Library discusses idempotent API design as a way to make automated retries safe.

## Budget the whole call chain

Suppose an edge request has a 600 ms deadline. Its authentication step consumes 50 ms and database work 150 ms, leaving at most 400 ms for a downstream call and response overhead. Setting every nested call's timeout to 600 ms guarantees that the edge deadline may expire first. Propagate an absolute deadline or remaining budget so deeper services stop work that no longer benefits the caller.

| Mechanism | Protects against | Risk if misused |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Timeout | Waiting forever | Too short causes false failures |
| Retry | Transient failure | Amplifies overload and duplicates |
| Backoff with jitter | Synchronized retry storms | Increases completion time |
| Idempotency key | Ambiguous repeat of one intent | Wrong key scope merges distinct intents |

## Limit retry amplification

If each of three service layers retries three times, a single user request can create up to 27 attempts at the deepest dependency. Choose one layer to retry a given operation when possible. Bound attempts, elapsed time, and retryable status classes. Exponential backoff spreads attempts; random jitter prevents many clients from waking at the same moment. When a dependency is overloaded, retries may worsen it. Respect server throttling signals and consider a retry budget or circuit breaker.

The idempotency store has its own design questions. What is the key scope: per account, operation type, or globally? What if the same key is reused with different payloads? How long must the key be remembered? If the operation remains pending, should a duplicate request wait, return pending, or query status? The durable operation and key record should commit in a way that survives process crashes. A key held only in memory does not protect a distributed service.

## Test the uncomfortable timing

Inject a failure immediately before commit, immediately after commit but before response, and during response write. Verify the client's retry gets the correct outcome in each case. Test concurrent duplicate requests, not just sequential retries. Measure retry rates, attempts per original call, and completion latency; a rising retry rate may be the first sign of downstream saturation.

## Design review

After a timeout, can the caller learn whether the operation happened? Which failures are retryable, at which layer, and for how long? Does the same intent keep the same idempotency key through every retry, including after a client restart?

## Sources

- [AWS Builders' Library: Making retries safe with idempotent APIs](https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/making-retries-safe-with-idempotent-APIs/)
- [AWS Prescriptive Guidance: Retry with backoff](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/cloud-design-patterns/retry-backoff.html)
02.10:
Batching groups several small operations into one larger operation. It can reduce fixed per-request overhead—network round trips, transaction setup, serialization headers, or broker calls—but makes each item wait for a batch and can create larger failure units. A good batch has explicit size, time, and memory bounds.

## Find the fixed cost

Suppose a worker inserts 1,000 analytics rows one at a time. Each insert pays a network round trip and database command overhead. Sending 100 rows per command reduces that overhead substantially. PostgreSQL supports multi-row `INSERT`; for very large loads, a bulk-copy path may be more suitable. The gain depends on row size, indexes, transaction log, and contention. Measure throughput and p99 latency rather than assuming the largest possible batch is best.

Kafka producers similarly accumulate records into batches per partition. A linger interval allows more records to arrive before sending, trading a little latency for fewer requests and better compression. If the application has strict per-message latency, a long linger is inappropriate even if throughput rises.

| Bound | Protects against | Tradeoff |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Maximum item count | Huge transaction or request | Small items may underfill byte budget |
| Maximum bytes | Memory and transport limits | Variable count per batch |
| Maximum wait | Unbounded low-traffic delay | More small batches |
| Maximum in-flight batches | Downstream overload | Producer may block or reject |

## Preserve per-item outcomes

A batch endpoint must define whether it is atomic. If one item is invalid, does the whole batch fail or are valid items accepted? For a database transaction, atomicity may be natural; for a notification send, partial success may be more useful. Return item-level IDs and errors so callers can retry only failed items. If a network timeout hides whether the batch committed, use idempotency keys per item or per batch with clear scope.

Ordering also matters. A batch containing updates to the same entity must preserve their intended order, or the consumer must compare versions. Sending many entities in one batch should not let one poison item stall all others forever. A repair path can split a failing batch to isolate the bad record, with limits to prevent endless retries.

## Balance throughput and latency

Imagine events arrive at 10/s and a batch holds 100. Waiting only for the count could delay the first item ten seconds. Add a maximum wait, perhaps 50 ms, so sparse traffic still moves. At 10,000/s the count fills quickly and the timer rarely matters. This count-or-time rule adapts to changing load. It must still respect memory and broker size limits.

Batching can worsen tail latency if a slow item holds the entire batch or if one large write monopolizes a connection. It can also increase lock duration and transaction log bursts. Run tests at both peak and quiet periods. Watch batch fill ratio, flush reason, item age, payload size, errors, and downstream saturation.

## Design review

Which fixed overhead is batching reducing? How long may the oldest item wait? What happens when one item fails, the response is lost, or the producer's buffer fills? Can the receiver report outcomes precisely enough for safe retry?

## Sources

- [PostgreSQL: `INSERT` command](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-insert.html)
- [Apache Kafka: Producer configuration](https://kafka.apache.org/10/configuration/producer-configs/)
02.11:
Backpressure is the signal that a downstream stage cannot safely accept work as fast as an upstream stage produces it. Without that signal, a queue or buffer grows until latency, memory use, or failure becomes unacceptable. Backpressure is a system property: every stage needs a bounded way to slow, reject, or persist excess work.

## Follow the flow of work

Consider an upload pipeline: client → API → object store → image processor. The client may send bytes faster than the API can forward them. A streaming API can pause reads when the downstream write buffer is full, then resume as capacity returns. Node.js streams expose this pattern; ignoring the writable stream's backpressure signal can accumulate large buffers and increase garbage collection or exhaust memory.

At the job level, a queue can absorb a temporary burst. But if arrival rate remains 2,000 jobs/s while processors complete 1,000 jobs/s, backlog grows by 1,000 every second. After one hour that is 3.6 million jobs. A queue smooths *bursts*; it does not fix sustained insufficient capacity. Calculate the backlog recovery time after a spike, including the normal ongoing arrival rate.

| Signal | Meaning | Possible response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Writable buffer full | Bytes cannot drain quickly | Pause upstream reads |
| Queue age rising | Work waits longer | Add consumers or reduce admission |
| DB pool wait rising | Too many concurrent queries | Limit in-flight requests |
| Memory near limit | Buffering too much state | Shed load before crash |

## Choose an overload policy

There are several valid responses: slow the sender, return `429` or `503`, drop low-value work, persist it for later, or degrade a feature. The right choice follows product semantics. A payment request should not be silently dropped. A live typing indicator can be skipped when stale. A report export can be accepted as a background job if status and eventual completion are visible.

Set queue limits by both item count and bytes; one giant job can exhaust memory despite a small count. Set time limits too: a request that waited in a queue for ten seconds may already be useless to its caller. Propagate deadlines and cancellation when possible. A bounded queue makes failure visible early enough for clients to back off, whereas an unbounded queue converts overload into a delayed collapse.

## Avoid pushing pressure elsewhere blindly

Adding more workers can overwhelm the database or provider they call. Put concurrency limits at the scarce dependency and measure its saturation. If the dependency is healthy but workers are too few, scale them. If it is already at capacity, admission control or priority may be the only safe immediate response. Retry storms can defeat backpressure by turning one rejected request into many attempts; use backoff and retry budgets.

Backpressure should be observable. Track incoming rate, completion rate, active work, oldest queued age, rejection count, memory, and downstream wait time. A flat queue depth can still be bad if producers and consumers are both stalled; pair depth with age and throughput.

## Design review

Where can the producer first learn the consumer is slow? What is the maximum buffered work in bytes and time? Which requests are rejected or degraded first? How long will backlog recovery take after the peak ends?

## Sources

- [Node.js: Backpressuring in Streams](https://nodejs.org/learn/modules/backpressuring-in-streams)
- [Google SRE: Handling Overload](https://sre.google/sre-book/handling-overload/)
02.12:
Tail latency is the slow end of a response-time distribution: p95, p99, or p99.9 rather than the average. It matters because real users experience individual requests, and a request that fans out to many components is more likely to encounter at least one unusually slow one. A design that looks fast at the median can still feel unreliable.

## See how fanout amplifies slow parts

Suppose a search request calls 20 independent shards and waits for all results. If each shard is slower than 200 ms on 1% of calls, the chance that at least one shard is slow is `1 - 0.99^20`, about 18%. Independence is a simplifying assumption, but the example shows why a small per-shard tail becomes a common end-to-end event. Google's “The Tail at Scale” describes this problem for large interactive systems.

Measure latency at the user-facing boundary and at each major stage. A 500 ms p99 could come from queue wait, garbage collection, a database lock, a cold cache, a network retransmission, or a slow shard. Aggregate histograms by endpoint and workload class. Mixing a cheap health check with a complex report query hides both experiences in one percentile. Compare peak and quiet periods separately.

| Technique | Helps when | Cost or caution |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Remove slow work from critical path | Work can finish later | Requires eventual-status contract |
| Bound fanout | Too many dependencies per request | May reduce completeness |
| Hedged request | Rare replica straggler | Extra load; must be safe to duplicate |
| Timeout and partial result | Some shards may be skipped | User sees incomplete result |
| Reduce utilization | Queueing dominates tail | More capacity cost |

## Treat queues as part of latency

When utilization approaches capacity, waiting time can rise sharply even if service time changes little. A worker that processes 100 requests/s cannot sustainably accept 110 requests/s; the queue grows. At a lower but bursty rate, a short peak can still create a long tail. Capacity planning should include headroom and workload variance, not just average CPU. Record queue wait separately from execution time so the fix targets the right stage.

Hedging a request to another replica after a delay can reduce stragglers, but it must have a limit and should generally be used for safe reads. Hedging writes without idempotency can duplicate effects. If every client hedges during overload, the additional traffic can make the tail worse. Choose a threshold based on measured latency distribution and use a global extra-work budget.

Partial results are a product decision. Search may return 95% of shard results with a visible indication if one shard times out; a financial balance cannot usually do that. Decide which components are required and which can be omitted. A deadline shared across the full request prevents one slow dependency from using all remaining time.

## Design review

What is the p99 of the user action, not just one service? How many independent dependencies does it wait for? Can a slow dependency be skipped, retried elsewhere, or moved out of the critical path? What extra load would the mitigation create during an incident?

## Sources

- [Dean and Barroso: The Tail at Scale](https://research.google/pubs/the-tail-at-scale/)
- [Google SRE: Service Level Objectives](https://sre.google/sre-book/service-level-objectives/)
02.13:
Load shedding deliberately rejects or omits some work before overload causes every request to fail slowly. It is a reliability mechanism for finite capacity. A fast, explicit rejection can preserve useful service for admitted requests and give callers a chance to back off.

## Recognize the overload point

A service has a sustainable throughput at a latency target, not an infinite capacity number. As incoming work approaches that rate, queues and tail latency often rise. If the system keeps accepting work, it may run out of memory or connection slots, time out most requests, and trigger retries that add even more load. Shed before the collapse point, using a signal that correlates with real saturation: in-flight work, queue age, CPU, database pool wait, or a combination.

Suppose a thumbnail service can process 800 images/s while meeting its SLO. A surge sends 1,500/s. If it accepts all jobs into an unbounded in-memory queue, the queue grows by 700/s and the oldest request becomes stale. If it admits only 800/s and returns a retryable rejection for the rest, admitted jobs can complete. The caller may retry later with backoff; if the work is optional, it may skip the thumbnail for now.

| Work class | Example policy | User impact |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Critical write | Reserve capacity or fail explicitly | Caller knows action did not complete |
| Interactive read | Short queue and deadline | Fast error or degraded view |
| Optional enrichment | Omit under pressure | Core response still works |
| Background task | Persist in bounded queue | Later completion with visible lag |

## Make priority and fairness explicit

Do not let a single tenant consume all capacity. Per-tenant limits or weighted fair queues can protect others. Reserve some capacity for health checks and administrative repair, but do not assume every request marked “high priority” can bypass limits. Priority rules should be simple enough to understand during an incident.

At the API boundary, choose an appropriate status such as `429` for client rate limits or `503` for temporary service overload, with documented retry guidance. Internally, the shedder should distinguish a request rejected before work starts from one whose side effect may have committed. If the outcome is ambiguous, the client needs an idempotency key or status query before retrying.

## Prevent a retry storm

Load shedding and client retries must agree. Immediate retry after a rejection recreates the same pressure. Use randomized backoff, cap attempts and elapsed time, and respect a server-provided retry delay where applicable. Consider a retry budget so additional attempts remain a small fraction of normal traffic. Monitor the accepted rate, rejected rate, completed rate, latency of admitted work, and downstream saturation together.

Test the policy with a ramped load test and with one backend missing. The desired outcome is stable latency for a useful fraction of requests, clear rejection for the rest, and rapid recovery when demand falls. Google's SRE guidance discusses shedding as a way to survive overload and avoid cascading failures; the mechanism should be practiced before a real surge.

## Design review

At what measured point does the service stop admitting work? Which work is protected, and which is rejected first? Will clients retry in a way that helps recovery? Can an operator tell whether the system is shedding by design or failing unexpectedly?

## Sources

- [Google SRE: Handling Overload](https://sre.google/sre-book/handling-overload/)
- [Google SRE: Addressing Cascading Failures](https://sre.google/sre-book/addressing-cascading-failures/)
03.01:
Relational database design starts with durable facts and the rules that connect them. Tables are not merely containers for API response objects. A useful schema identifies entities, stable keys, relationships, constraints, and the transactions that keep business invariants true under concurrent writes.

## Model facts, not screens

Consider a ticket-booking product. Core facts include an event, a seat, a customer, and a reservation. A reservation has its own identity and state; it is not just a `booked=true` flag on a seat because it must record who booked, when a hold expires, and what happened during payment. A normalized first pass might use `events`, `seats`, `customers`, and `reservations` with foreign keys between them.

Write the invariants before the columns. A seat may have at most one active reservation at a time. A reservation must point to an existing seat and customer. A confirmed reservation must preserve the price that was accepted, even if event pricing changes later. Some rules can be represented by `NOT NULL`, `CHECK`, `UNIQUE`, and foreign key constraints. Others require a transaction or carefully designed partial unique index. Database constraints protect against races and alternative write paths that bypass application checks.

| Fact | Likely key | Important constraint |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Event | `event_id` | Valid start time and owner |
| Seat | `seat_id` | Unique label within event |
| Reservation | `reservation_id` | References seat and customer |
| Payment attempt | `attempt_id` | Idempotency key unique in scope |

## Choose key and relationship semantics

Use stable identifiers that do not change when a display name changes. A seat label such as `A-12` is meaningful within an event, but may not be globally unique. A compound uniqueness rule `(event_id, seat_label)` captures that domain fact. Foreign keys prevent dangling references, but deletion policies need thought: deleting a customer record may be legally required, while a financial transaction might need retained non-personal audit data. Decide whether to restrict, cascade, anonymize, or archive rather than accepting defaults blindly.

Many-to-many relationships usually need a join table that can carry its own facts. An event may have many organizers and an organizer may manage many events; `event_organizers` can store role and assignment time. If the relationship has lifecycle or attributes, treating it as an explicit entity often clarifies the model.

## Design transactions around invariants

Two customers can click the same seat at once. The application may check availability, but both checks can observe “free.” The write must resolve the race using a lock, conditional update, exclusion or uniqueness rule, or serializable transaction appropriate to the database. Return a clear conflict to the loser. A transaction should include all local changes that must commit together, such as reservation and audit record. External payment cannot be covered by a local database transaction, so the workflow needs explicit pending states and recovery.

Normalization reduces duplication and update anomalies, but it is not a ban on derived data. A read-heavy seat map may use a materialized projection or cache while the reservation table remains authoritative. Keep derived views rebuildable. Denormalize only after identifying a query or latency need and deciding how updates propagate.

## Validate with real queries

List the important operations: available seats for one event, a customer's upcoming reservations, and one reservation by ID. Design indexes for those access paths and test representative row counts. A clean schema that needs a full scan for every common operation is not finished. Conversely, adding an index to every column increases write and storage cost. Use query plans and measurements to refine the first model.

## Design review

What facts must survive independently? Which rules are enforced by the database even when two writers race? Which data is authoritative, and which is a projection? Can you explain each deletion rule and common query path?

03.02:
A relational database can serve a key-value API effectively when the workload is mainly point reads, conditional writes, and bounded scans. The first design is often one table with a primary key, value, version, and expiration field. The hard part is the contract around concurrency, size, TTL, and durability, not writing `SELECT ... WHERE key = ?`.

## Define the key-value contract

Suppose clients call `put(namespace, key, value)`, `get(namespace, key)`, and `delete(namespace, key)`. Is a key unique globally or only within a namespace? Does `put` overwrite unconditionally, create only if absent, or compare a version? What is the maximum value size? Does a missing key differ from an expired key? Are range scans or prefix queries required? These answers determine the primary key and indexes.

A simple SQL shape is `PRIMARY KEY (namespace, key)` with `value BYTEA`, `version BIGINT`, and `expires_at TIMESTAMPTZ`. A point read uses the composite key. If clients need optimistic concurrency, an update can include `WHERE version = expected_version` and increment the version; zero updated rows means conflict or absence, which may require a follow-up check. A create-if-absent operation can use a uniqueness constraint and `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT` behavior.

| Operation | SQL-level idea | Edge case |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Get | Primary-key lookup | Expired row still physically present |
| Put | Insert/upsert | Concurrent overwrite semantics |
| Compare-and-set | Conditional version update | Conflict versus missing key |
| Delete | Delete or tombstone | Retry and recreation race |
| Expire | Filter on `expires_at` plus cleanup | Cleanup lag and clock source |

## Treat TTL as two separate behaviors

Logical expiration means a `get` does not return a row after its deadline. Physical cleanup removes old rows to reclaim space. The cleanup job can lag without violating logical expiration if reads filter expired rows. But large numbers of expired rows still cost storage and index maintenance, so monitor cleanup lag and batch deletes. Use the database's time consistently for writes and reads if client clocks cannot be trusted.

If keys may be recreated, a delayed delete or stale worker must not remove the new value. Conditional deletion by version or expiration timestamp protects against that race. The same issue appears in cache invalidation and lease expiry: identity and version matter more than a bare key.

## Set realistic limits

SQL offers transactions and mature durability, but huge values are a poor fit for the hot row path. Put large objects in object storage and keep a pointer and metadata in SQL if necessary. Point lookups scale well with a primary-key index until working set, I/O, or write throughput becomes limiting. A hot key can still serialize many conditional writes. More application replicas will not remove contention on the same row.

For a small to moderate service, SQL may be operationally simpler than adding a dedicated distributed key-value store. If the workload later needs extremely high write rates across many independent keys, partition by a stable key and plan data movement. If it needs ordered range scans, random hash sharding can make those scans expensive. Let the required API shape guide distribution.

## Design review

Does `put` mean replace, create, or compare-and-set? Can clients safely retry after a timeout? What happens when a key expires but cleanup has not run? How do you prevent an old cleanup task from deleting a recreated key?

03.03:
An index is an extra data structure that helps a database find or order rows without scanning every row. It is valuable when a query selects a small or useful subset, but it consumes storage and makes writes do more work. Design indexes from actual predicates, sorting, and data distribution, then confirm that the planner uses them at realistic scale.

## Begin with one query

Suppose a booking page runs `SELECT id, starts_at FROM reservations WHERE customer_id = ? AND status = 'CONFIRMED' ORDER BY starts_at DESC LIMIT 20`. An index beginning with `customer_id`, then `status`, then `starts_at DESC` can support filtering and ordering for that shape. An index on `starts_at` alone may not help much if the database still must examine many other customers' rows. A primary-key index on `id` helps a different query: fetching one reservation by ID.

The order of columns in a composite index matters. Equality conditions on leading columns often narrow the search, while a following range or sort column helps traverse the matching slice. The exact planner behavior depends on the database and query; do not apply a memorized ordering rule without checking `EXPLAIN`. PostgreSQL documents B-tree indexes for equality and range comparisons and has detailed guidance for multicolumn indexes.

| Query pattern | Candidate index | Caveat |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `WHERE id = ?` | Primary key | Usually already exists |
| `WHERE customer_id = ? ORDER BY created_at` | `(customer_id, created_at)` | Direction and limit affect plan |
| `WHERE lower(email) = ?` | Expression index on `lower(email)` | Must match query expression |
| Search inside JSON | GIN or targeted expression index | Depends on operator and selectivity |

## Understand selectivity and cost

If a condition matches 90% of a table, an index may be slower than a sequential scan because it creates many scattered heap reads. If it matches ten rows among millions, an index is often valuable. Statistics help the query planner estimate row counts and choose a path. Stale statistics or skewed values can lead to poor plans. Use `EXPLAIN` to see estimates and `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` carefully to see actual behavior; remember that the latter executes the query, which matters for writes.

An index can sometimes satisfy a query's selected columns without reading the main table, but this depends on visibility and database-specific behavior. Covering indexes may improve a hot read at the cost of a larger index. Partial indexes can index only rows matching a stable predicate such as `status = 'ACTIVE'`, reducing size when most rows are inactive. These are targeted tools, not default additions.

## Account for the write path

Each inserted or updated row may require work in every affected index. A table with many indexes can have slower writes, more log volume, longer migrations, and higher storage cost. Update-heavy columns in indexes are especially expensive. Drop unused indexes only after measuring their real usage and accounting for infrequent jobs. When building an index on a large live table, use the database's online/concurrent option and understand its lock and failure behavior.

The index also cannot fix a query whose predicate prevents its use, such as wrapping an indexed column in an unindexed expression or requesting an unanchored substring search with a plain B-tree. Sometimes the better fix is a query rewrite, a different index type, or a dedicated search index.

## Design review

Which exact query is this index for? How many rows does its predicate match at production scale? Does the plan use the index and avoid an expensive sort? What write cost and migration time does it add?

03.04:
A B-tree is a balanced, ordered index that keeps keys in pages and lets a database narrow a search through several levels. Its value is not only fast equality lookup: ordered leaves also support ranges, prefix scans, and sometimes `ORDER BY` without a separate sort. Understanding the page structure makes index choices and write costs easier to reason about.

## Follow a lookup through the tree

Imagine an index on `(customer_id, created_at)` for an orders table. A lookup for one customer's recent orders starts at the root page, follows separator keys through internal pages, and reaches a leaf page containing key entries and row references. It can then walk adjacent entries in key order until it has enough rows. Because each page contains many keys, the tree has high fanout and stays shallow even for large tables. The balance property means growth adds levels gradually rather than turning lookups into a long chain.

An equality search on `customer_id` finds a contiguous region. Adding a time range or descending order can use the second key in that region. Reversing the index to `(created_at, customer_id)` changes which entries are adjacent, so the same query may inspect far more keys. This is why composite index order follows the query shape, not the column order in a table.

| Query | B-tree fit | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `id = 42` | Strong | Direct ordered-key lookup |
| `created_at BETWEEN a AND b` | Strong | Scan a bounded key range |
| `ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 20` | Often strong | Read leading ordered entries |
| `name LIKE 'ann%'` | Conditional | Prefix can form a range with suitable collation/operator class |
| `name LIKE '%ann%'` | Poor | Leading wildcard has no narrow starting point |

PostgreSQL's index-type documentation describes B-trees as suitable for equality and range comparisons; its detailed B-tree documentation describes the multilevel balanced implementation. A database planner may still choose a full scan when most rows match, because following the index and fetching many scattered table rows can cost more.

## Account for inserts and updates

An insert finds the correct leaf page and adds an entry. If the page lacks room, the tree may split it and update parent separator information. A split is local, but it still writes pages and log records. Updating an indexed key can require a new index entry; maintaining many B-trees makes writes and storage more expensive. Duplicate values also create many entries, though PostgreSQL may compress duplicate leaf entries with deduplication in eligible cases.

An index entry typically points to a row or tuple location rather than containing every requested field. Fetching table rows can dominate a query if it returns many results. An index-only scan may avoid some table access when the database can verify visibility and the index contains needed data, but this depends on engine details and workload. Do not assume that “uses index” means “fast”; inspect actual row counts, heap fetches, and I/O.

## Keep the abstraction honest

B-tree diagrams often show one key per node; production indexes store many keys per page and manage concurrency, page splits, deleted entries, and recovery. The useful mental model is ordered pages plus a shallow search path. It predicts why a range query is natural, why a leading wildcard is not, and why random inserts can cause more page churn than an append-like key pattern. It does not predict a query plan without data statistics and cost estimates.

## Design review

For a proposed index, identify the leading equality keys, the first range key, and the rows the query must return. Can the scan stop early? How many table fetches remain? What extra work will each write create?

03.05:
A query planner chooses an execution plan: how to find rows, join relations, sort results, and aggregate values. SQL says what result is wanted; the plan determines how much work is done. A slow query is often a poor plan for the current data distribution, a missing access path, or a query that asks for more rows than the user needs.

## Read the plan as a tree of work

Suppose a dashboard asks for a customer's last twenty paid orders. The planner may use an index scan on `orders(customer_id, created_at)`, filter `status = 'PAID'`, and stop at twenty. Or it may scan many orders, sort them, and apply a limit. `EXPLAIN` displays the chosen plan and its estimates. Read from the leaf operations upward: scans feed joins, filters, sorts, and the final result.

Pay attention to estimated rows, actual rows, loops, and timing when available. If a nested-loop join expects one row from its outer side but actually receives 100,000, the repeated inner lookup can dominate execution. If the estimate is wrong, statistics may be stale or the data may be skewed or correlated in a way ordinary column statistics do not capture. If estimates are accurate but the plan is still slow, the query may genuinely need a new index or a different shape.

| Plan symptom | Possible cause | First investigation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sequential scan on huge table | Predicate not selective or no usable index | Compare rows matched and index options |
| Large sort before `LIMIT` | Index cannot provide order | Check composite index order |
| Join output far above estimate | Skew or correlation | Inspect statistics and predicates |
| Many loops of inner scan | Bad join order or missing inner index | Multiply actual loops by per-loop work |
| Disk spill | Sort/hash exceeds memory | Reduce rows or adjust memory carefully |

## Distinguish cost units from time

PostgreSQL plan costs are relative estimates used to compare candidate plans; they are not milliseconds. An `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` execution reports actual timing and row counts. It executes the statement, so running it on an `UPDATE` or `DELETE` can change data unless wrapped and rolled back appropriately. For production diagnosis, consider query impact, sensitive parameters, and sampling. Compare plans with representative values because one customer with five orders may choose a very different plan from one with five million.

`ANALYZE` refreshes statistical summaries that inform estimates. It samples data, so estimates can still be wrong for rare or highly skewed values. A planner may choose a sequential scan deliberately when a filter returns a large fraction of a table. Forcing index use without understanding cost can make the query slower.

## Fix the cause, then validate

Possible remedies include a more selective predicate, a composite or partial index, a query rewrite, an updated statistic, or a read model for expensive aggregation. Limit the selected columns and rows when the user does not need everything. Avoid making a query faster in isolation while shifting huge write cost into indexes or materialization. Compare before and after with the same data volume and realistic parameter mix, then monitor p95/p99 under load.

The plan is evidence, not a verdict. It explains what the database chose under current estimates and settings. The product requirement still decides whether the response is fast enough and whether a more expensive write path is worthwhile.

## Design review

Which operation consumes most rows or time? Do estimated and actual row counts differ substantially? Does the plan change for hot customers or recent dates? What new cost would the proposed fix add to writes and storage?

03.06:
Database locks and isolation levels determine how concurrent transactions interact. The goal is to preserve business invariants without serializing unrelated work. A transaction can be individually correct in a single-user test and still fail when two users act at the same time.

## Name the race

Suppose a booking service allows one reservation per seat. Two requests read “available,” then both attempt to reserve. A read check followed by an unprotected write is not enough. A unique constraint on active seat ownership, a conditional update, or a row lock can make one writer win. The right mechanism depends on the schema and whether several rows together form the invariant.

Locks can be implicit: an `UPDATE` holds row-level locks on changed rows until its transaction completes. A `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` can reserve rows for a planned change. Table locks may appear during schema changes or some maintenance. Long transactions extend lock hold time and can block unrelated work. Keep external network calls, user think time, and slow report queries out of a write transaction where possible.

## Know what an isolation level promises

At PostgreSQL's default **Read Committed**, each statement sees a snapshot from the start of that statement. A second query within the same transaction may see a newly committed value. **Repeatable Read** keeps a stable transaction snapshot, but it can still allow certain write-skew patterns. **Serializable** aims for an outcome equivalent to some serial order and may abort one transaction with a serialization failure; the application must retry the whole transaction safely. PostgreSQL's implementation treats Read Uncommitted like Read Committed and offers stronger phantom protection in Repeatable Read than the SQL minimum.

| Anomaly | Example | Typical protection |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lost update | Two writers overwrite one balance | Version check or row lock |
| Nonrepeatable read | Re-read sees new committed value | Stable snapshot when required |
| Write skew | Two doctors both go off call after checking the other | Serializable transaction or explicit invariant lock |
| Deadlock | Two transactions lock rows in opposite order | Consistent lock order and retry |

The isolation label alone does not enforce every domain rule. A unique index is often the clearest protection for a uniqueness invariant. A cross-row rule may need serializable isolation or a single row representing the shared constraint. Choose a strategy that can be explained with a concrete concurrent timeline.

## Handle conflicts as normal outcomes

Deadlocks and serialization failures can be expected under contention. Retry the entire transaction with bounded attempts and backoff, after ensuring external side effects are not duplicated. A payment call inside a retried database transaction is dangerous: the database can roll back while the payment remains real. Use a durable workflow state and idempotent external API instead.

Measure lock wait time, blocked sessions, transaction age, deadlocks, and serialization failures. A spike in lock waits may indicate a hot row, an overly broad update, or a migration holding a lock. Indexes can shorten the rows a write scans, indirectly reducing lock duration, but they also add write work. Inspect the actual SQL and plan before changing isolation globally.

## Design review

Write down two concurrent requests step by step. Which statement blocks or fails? What invariant prevents both from committing? If a transaction is retried, are all its side effects safe to repeat? How long could a lock be held during a dependency timeout?

03.07:
Multi-version concurrency control, or MVCC, lets readers see a consistent snapshot while writers create newer row versions. In PostgreSQL, ordinary reads generally do not block ordinary writes, and ordinary writes do not block reads. The tradeoff is that old row versions must be tracked and eventually reclaimed, and a snapshot does not automatically make every multi-row business rule safe.

## Follow a row through an update

Imagine an account row with `status = 'ACTIVE'`. Transaction A starts a read. Transaction B changes the status to `SUSPENDED` and commits. A's visible value depends on its isolation level and when its snapshot was taken. The database keeps enough version information for A to see the appropriate state while newer transactions may see B's change. This avoids forcing B to wait for every reader before it can write.

In PostgreSQL, Read Committed takes a new snapshot per statement, so A's second statement may see the new status. Repeatable Read uses a stable transaction snapshot. This is a visibility rule, not a promise that a business workflow can ignore conflicts. If two transactions read different rows and then update them based on each other's old values, both may commit under snapshot isolation and violate a cross-row invariant. Serializable isolation or an explicit coordination point may be needed.

| Concern | MVCC effect | Remaining obligation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Reader versus writer | Read sees a consistent version | Choose needed freshness/isolation |
| Writer versus writer | Conflicts still occur | Handle waits and retries |
| Old versions | Retained while potentially visible | Vacuum and transaction hygiene |
| Long snapshot | Keeps older state accessible | Can delay cleanup and cause bloat |

## Understand cleanup cost

Updating or deleting rows leaves versions that cannot be reclaimed while an old transaction may still need them. PostgreSQL's vacuum machinery eventually reclaims dead tuples and maintains visibility information. A long-running transaction can pin an old snapshot and make cleanup less effective, increasing table and index size. That can turn a read-heavy workload into an I/O problem over time. Monitor transaction age, dead tuples, vacuum progress, and relation growth.

MVCC also interacts with indexes. An index may point to a tuple that is no longer visible to the current snapshot, so the engine may need a heap visibility check. This is one reason an index-only scan is conditional rather than guaranteed by index contents alone. Freshly updated tables may behave differently from mostly static tables.

## Do not confuse snapshots with replication

MVCC describes concurrent visibility inside a database instance. It does not by itself say how current a read replica is or whether a write survives a host failure. Replication lag and durability are separate contracts. Likewise, a snapshot does not make a distributed workflow atomic across services. Keep each promise separate in a design review.

A useful mental model is “many logical versions, each transaction reads the version allowed by its snapshot.” The actual storage engine uses transaction IDs, visibility rules, and cleanup machinery. The model predicts why reads can coexist with writes and why a forgotten open transaction can have system-wide cost.

## Design review

What snapshot does each statement see? Could two writers both make a decision from stale but internally consistent snapshots? How are conflicts detected? What operational signal shows that old versions are accumulating?

03.08:
A write-ahead log (WAL) records changes before modified data pages are written to their final locations. It is central to crash recovery: after a process or machine failure, the database can replay durable log records to restore changes that had not yet reached table and index files. WAL also supports replication and point-in-time recovery, but each use has separate retention and failure considerations.

## Trace one commit

Suppose a transaction inserts an order and updates inventory. The database changes in-memory pages and appends log records describing the modifications. Before it acknowledges a durable commit, the relevant log must be flushed according to its commit policy. The data pages can be written later. If the process crashes after acknowledgment but before those pages are flushed, recovery starts from a checkpoint and replays the log to restore the committed state.

The ordering rule matters: if a data page reached disk before its log record was durable, a crash could leave a change the recovery process cannot reason about. PostgreSQL's WAL documentation states that data-file changes are written only after the describing log records are flushed. Sequential log writes and group commit make this cheaper than forcing every modified table page to disk at each commit.

| Component | Role | Failure question |
| --- | --- | --- |
| WAL record | Describes a change | Was it flushed before success? |
| Checkpoint | Limits redo starting point | How much log must replay? |
| Data page | Holds table/index state | Was it written before crash? |
| WAL archive | Preserves history beyond local segments | Can a backup replay to desired time? |

## Separate local durability from disaster recovery

A local WAL flush protects against a process crash and some host failures, depending on storage guarantees. It is not a substitute for backups: accidental deletion, storage loss, or corruption can affect both data and local WAL. A physical backup plus archived WAL can restore to a selected time within the retained log range. Test restore, including the target time, rather than assuming archived files are sufficient.

Replication often streams WAL or related change records to followers. If acknowledgment does not wait for a follower, a primary failure may lose its most recent acknowledged writes when the lagging follower is promoted. If acknowledgment waits for remote durability, write latency and availability depend on that follower. State the exact durability promise and promotion policy.

## Plan for log growth and lag

WAL is not an unlimited queue. A slow replica or broken archive destination can cause old segments to be retained, filling disk. Large bulk updates, index builds, and schema changes can generate substantial log volume. Monitor WAL generation rate, archive failures, replication lag, and available space. Set alarms early enough to intervene without an emergency deletion that destroys recovery options.

Recovery time also matters. Long intervals between checkpoints can mean more replay work after a crash; very frequent checkpoints can increase write pressure. The right settings depend on workload and recovery objective. A design should estimate both data-loss bound and time-to-restore, then verify them in drills.

## Design review

When does the client receive success relative to WAL flush and replica acknowledgment? What can be lost after a process, host, or region failure? Can backups plus retained WAL actually restore to the required point, and how long does replay take?

03.09:
A database ticket server issues unique identifiers from a small, centralized sequence so many data shards can create records without colliding. It separates **ID allocation** from **record storage**. This is attractive when shards need compact numeric primary keys and records may move between shards, but it puts every new ID on an availability and throughput path to the allocator.

## Why shard-local counters are insufficient

Suppose a photo service stores users across ten independent databases. Each database can auto-increment a local photo ID, but all ten can produce `photo_id = 42`. That ID cannot uniquely identify a photo in a global API unless every request also carries the shard identity. If data later moves between shards, a global ID simplifies references and migration. One approach is a dedicated sequence service that returns a new number before the photo is inserted into its shard.

Flickr described a concrete ticket-server design for globally unique integer IDs across MySQL shards. A small table on a dedicated server advanced an auto-increment value, and two independent servers used disjoint odd and even ranges. The key idea is disjoint allocation: the two issuers cannot return the same number even if they do not replicate each generated ID. This trades a single global sequence order for availability and compactness.

| Option | Strength | Important cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One central sequence | Simple global uniqueness | Network hop and allocator dependency |
| Two disjoint sequences | Failure tolerance without per-ID replication | Gaps and no single issuance order |
| Allocate ranges to app nodes | Fewer allocator calls | Lost unused ranges on crash |
| Random UUID | No central issuer | Larger keys and index locality tradeoff |
| Time-based ID | Distributed and roughly ordered | Clock and worker-ID management |

## Define what the ID promises

Uniqueness is different from consecutiveness and time order. A database sequence may skip values after rollback, caching, or process failure. A ticket server should promise “unique within this namespace,” not “every integer appears.” If the product requires strict event order, a ticket number alone may be insufficient because an ID can be allocated before its transaction commits. A later ID may become visible first.

Scope matters. Separate sequences for photos and comments can reduce contention and allow different growth rates, but the pair `(entity_type, id)` may then be the true global key. For API exposure, use opaque IDs if clients should not infer traffic volumes or creation time. A compact internal integer can be mapped to another public representation when necessary.

## Design the failure path

If the allocator is unavailable, can writes continue with preallocated ranges? A range allocator gives each writer a block, such as 1,000 IDs, and replenishes before it runs out. That reduces request rate to the central service but means a crashed node may waste unused IDs. Prevent range overlap by committing ownership durably. If a recovered node restarts with stale local state, it must not reuse IDs from a prior lease.

Monitor issuance rate, p99 allocation latency, remaining range headroom, sequence exhaustion horizon, and collisions at the storage layer. A unique constraint on the destination table remains a valuable last line of defense. The allocator design should be load tested at the projected *write* rate, including retry storms.

## Design review

What is the exact uniqueness namespace? Are gaps acceptable? What happens when one issuer is down? Can an ID be allocated but its record fail to commit, and does that affect any caller's assumptions?

03.10:
Relational database scaling is a sequence of workload-specific decisions. A database can hit limits in CPU, memory, disk I/O, storage size, connection count, write contention, or recovery time. “Add replicas” helps some read workloads but does not make one hot row or a single primary's write path scale indefinitely.

## Locate the limiting work

Suppose an order database shows rising p99 latency. First separate query classes and inspect plans, indexes, lock waits, buffer hit rate, disk throughput, and connection-pool wait. An unindexed query can consume far more resources than the rest of the traffic; fixing it may buy more capacity than a new server. A large number of idle connections can also impose memory overhead without increasing useful throughput. Right-size pools and keep transactions short.

Vertical scaling gives more CPU, memory, or I/O to one database and may be the simplest next step. It has a ceiling and may require a failover or restart. Read replicas can serve queries that tolerate replication lag, such as a browsing page, while the primary continues accepting writes. A read-after-write path may need to stay on the primary or use a lag-aware routing policy. PostgreSQL's hot standby supports read-only queries; the application still decides which reads may be stale.

| Pressure | Candidate response | New tradeoff |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Expensive query | Rewrite/index/materialized view | Maintenance and freshness |
| CPU or memory limit | Larger instance | Larger failure domain and cost |
| Read-heavy traffic | Read replicas | Lag and routing complexity |
| Old time-series data | Partition by time | Partition management and cross-range queries |
| Write throughput by key | Shard by stable key | Cross-shard queries and migrations |

## Use partitioning for a clear access pattern

Table partitioning splits a logical table into physical pieces. Time partitions can make retention cheap—drop an old partition rather than delete millions of rows—and let the planner prune irrelevant partitions for date-bounded queries. But every query must use the partition key effectively to benefit. Too many tiny partitions increase metadata and planning overhead. A partitioned table on one machine also does not add machine-level write capacity by itself.

Sharding distributes data across independent database nodes. Choose a key aligned with common transactions, such as `tenant_id`, so most operations stay on one shard. Cross-shard joins, global uniqueness, rebalancing, and hot tenants become explicit application concerns. Use logical shards or a routing map if physical placement may change. A hash of the key may balance ordinary tenants but cannot solve a single tenant that dominates traffic.

## Keep reliability in the scaling plan

Replicas need monitored lag and tested promotion. A failover can change the last acknowledged write visible on the new primary depending on replication mode. Backups and restore drills remain necessary even with replicas because a bad delete can replicate too. As the dataset grows, restore time may become the real scaling limit before query throughput does. Estimate recovery time and data-loss bounds alongside QPS.

Scale in measured steps: remove waste, tune the hot paths, add suitable capacity, then partition where the workload proves it necessary. Each step should have a threshold and a rollback plan. “We may have millions of users” is not enough to justify distributed writes before query and traffic data exist.

## Design review

Which resource is saturated first? Which operations can read stale replicas? Does the proposed partition key keep the important transaction local? How long will backup restore and failover take at the projected data size?

03.11:
An online index build adds a new access path while a table continues serving production traffic. The challenge is that rows can change during the build. The database must capture those concurrent changes and validate that the finished index covers a consistent state. “Online” reduces blocking, but it does not mean zero resource use or zero operational risk.

## Why a normal build can hurt

On a large orders table, a standard index build scans the table and constructs index pages. In PostgreSQL, ordinary `CREATE INDEX` allows reads but blocks writes until completion. If the table is busy, a build lasting minutes or hours can create an unacceptable write outage. `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` allows inserts, updates, and deletes to proceed, making it suitable for many live changes.

The concurrent path performs more work. PostgreSQL documents two table scans and waits for relevant existing transactions. CPU, I/O, WAL, and cache pressure can raise normal query latency even though writes are not blocked by the build lock. A long-running transaction may delay progress. Schedule and monitor the migration with peak traffic and headroom in mind.

| Phase or concern | What to check |
| --- | --- |
| Before build | Query need, estimated index size, disk and WAL headroom |
| During build | Progress view, I/O, p99 latency, lock waits |
| After build | Index valid, planner uses it, query actually improves |
| Failure | Invalid index cleanup or rebuild plan |

## Treat uniqueness as a migration

A unique index cannot be built successfully if duplicates already exist. First query for duplicates and decide how to resolve them. During a concurrent unique build, new writes may begin seeing uniqueness errors before the index is fully valid. If the build later fails, an invalid index may remain and still impose write overhead; inspect catalog state and clean it up before retrying. This is more involved than adding a plain read index.

If the application also needs a new constraint or changed write logic, stage the rollout. Deploy code that tolerates the new rule, clean existing data, build the index, verify it, then make code rely on the invariant. The exact order depends on whether older application versions may still write duplicate data. A rolling deployment means old and new writers coexist for a while.

## Validate the useful result

An index can be valid yet unused. Run the target query with representative parameters and inspect `EXPLAIN` or `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`. If the planner chooses a sequential scan because the predicate matches most rows, the index may not help. Check write overhead too: an index that saves 20 ms on a rare report but slows every insert may be a poor tradeoff.

For partitioned tables, online indexing may require per-partition steps and a metadata-level parent operation rather than one concurrent command. Confirm the database version's supported behavior before writing a migration script. Keep the script idempotent and observable; restarting a failed build without checking an invalid artifact can leave the system worse off.

## Design review

What query justifies the index? Will the build block writes, and how much extra I/O can it create? What happens if duplicates or a deadlock make it fail? How will you prove the new index is valid, used, and worth its ongoing write cost?

03.12:
Schema evolution changes stored data and application contracts while old and new software versions may run at the same time. A safe migration is a sequence of compatible steps, not one large `ALTER TABLE` followed by a hope that every process updates instantly. The desired final schema matters, but the intermediate states determine whether a live rollout works.

## Use expand, migrate, contract

Suppose an orders table has `customer_name` and you want a structured `customer_id` foreign key. First **expand**: add a nullable `customer_id` column and deploy readers that can handle either representation. Then **migrate**: make new writes populate `customer_id`, backfill existing rows in bounded batches, and compare records. Finally **contract**: switch all reads to the new field, enforce a non-null or foreign-key constraint when data is ready, and remove the old column after old binaries are gone. Fowler calls this parallel change, or expand and contract.

The stages overlap with deployments. If older app instances still write only `customer_name`, the backfill can finish and immediately fall behind again. Either dual-write during the transition or route writes through one compatible version; monitor the count of rows still missing the new field. Dual writes within one database transaction are easier to reason about than cross-database dual writes, but read preference and conflict behavior still need definition.

| Change | Safer intermediate state | Common mistake |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Add field | Nullable or compatible default first | Require it before old writers know it |
| Rename field | Write/read both during migration | Drop old name in one deployment |
| Change type | New column, transform, compare | In-place rewrite at peak without estimate |
| Add constraint | Clean data, validate, then enforce | Assume existing rows already comply |
| Remove field | Wait for usage telemetry | Delete while an old worker still reads it |

## Control database work

Some DDL is metadata-only; other operations scan or rewrite large tables or take locks. The behavior depends on database version, column default, type change, and constraint. PostgreSQL documents that many table modifications are possible through `ALTER TABLE`, but operational impact must be checked for the exact statement. Test on a production-sized copy, set lock timeouts where appropriate, and monitor replication lag and WAL volume. A migration that is fast on ten thousand rows can be disruptive on a billion.

Backfill in small batches ordered by stable key, with a checkpoint so it can resume. Avoid one transaction that holds locks and retains old row versions for hours. Record transformed-row counts, errors, and reconciliation mismatches. If the transformation is ambiguous, define manual or product-level rules rather than silently inventing data.

## Make rollback realistic

Rollback is easiest during expansion because the old representation still exists. Once old data is dropped or new writes use semantics the old version cannot understand, rolling back code may be unsafe. Define the rollback point for each phase. It may be safer to roll forward a fix after contract than to restore an old binary.

## Design review

Can old and new application versions run together at every step? What writes occur during backfill? How will you prove all rows and consumers have migrated? At which point does rollback stop being a simple code revert?

03.13:
Soft delete marks a record as deleted without immediately removing its row. It can support recovery, audit, and asynchronous cleanup, but it changes the meaning of every query and uniqueness rule. The core question is what “deleted” promises to users: hidden from normal views, restorable for a period, or eventually erased from all systems.

## Define the lifecycle

For a project-management app, a task might move from `ACTIVE` to `TRASHED`, remain restorable for 30 days, then be permanently deleted. A `deleted_at` timestamp can represent the transition and support a cleanup job. But a task also has comments, attachments, search documents, cache entries, and analytics events. Decide which derived views hide it immediately, which retain it for recovery, and what physical deletion entails.

Normal reads must consistently filter `deleted_at IS NULL`. One forgotten query can expose trashed data. Centralizing common query scopes can help, but test every path, including joins, exports, administrative tools, and search. A soft-deleted parent with live children needs a rule: hide children, cascade the soft delete, or allow them to remain independently visible. The rule should be expressed in domain behavior, not inferred from a database flag.

| Concern | Design question | Typical mechanism |
| --- | --- | --- |
| User visibility | When does the record disappear? | Filter and cache invalidation |
| Uniqueness | Can a new record reuse its name? | Partial unique index on active rows |
| Restore | What if the name was reused? | Conflict resolution or new name |
| Retention | When is physical cleanup allowed? | Bounded purge job |
| Privacy deletion | Must all copies be erased? | Data inventory and verified deletion |

## Revisit constraints and indexes

Suppose usernames are unique while active. A global unique index on `username` prevents reuse after soft delete. A partial unique index such as `UNIQUE(username) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL` can express active-only uniqueness in PostgreSQL. Restoring an old user may then fail if another active user claimed the name. That is a valid conflict requiring a product decision, not a database bug.

An index on active rows can also keep common reads efficient when most historical rows are deleted. But the planner uses a partial index only when it can prove a query implies its predicate. Keep query conditions explicit and inspect plans. Soft delete is an update, so it creates normal write and WAL work; a large mass-delete operation can still be expensive.

## Do not substitute soft delete for backup or erasure

Soft delete helps undo accidental user actions within a defined window. It does not protect against database loss or malicious changes, so backups remain necessary. Conversely, retaining a row indefinitely may violate a product's promised deletion or a legal retention rule. Physical purge must include derived stores, object storage, replicas, and backups according to the relevant policy. Avoid promising instant erasure if backup expiry is the actual limit.

Operationally, monitor the number and age of trashed records, purge failures, storage growth, and restore conflicts. Make purge idempotent, since retries may happen after a partial cleanup. Keep audit records only as long as policy permits and avoid copying sensitive payloads into logs that escape the deletion process.

## Design review

What exactly does a user see after delete? Which queries and derived views must change? Can a deleted unique value be reused, and what happens on restore? When and how is the row physically removed from every required location?

04.01:
“NoSQL” is a broad label for data stores with different models and tradeoffs. It is not a single alternative to relational databases. The useful question is which operations must be fast and correct: point lookups, document retrieval, ordered scans, relationship traversal, or large analytical aggregation. Choose the data model and distribution strategy from those access patterns.

## Begin with queries and invariants

Suppose a commerce system stores orders. It needs to create an order with line items, list recent orders for one customer, update fulfillment state, and produce finance reports. A relational database may handle the core transaction well because constraints and joins express important invariants. A document store could keep one order and its line items together if they are usually read and changed as one unit. A key-value store could serve a read-through copy by order ID, but it would not by itself answer a flexible finance report.

Write the required operations before evaluating products. Include key cardinality, item size, query predicates, sorting, update frequency, transactional scope, consistency target, and retention. DynamoDB's modeling guidance explicitly begins from the questions the application must answer. The model can be excellent for known key-based paths while making an ad hoc query unexpectedly expensive.

| Need | Candidate model | Design question |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One object by exact key | Key-value | How is key distributed and expired? |
| Related fields read together | Document | Does the document grow without bound? |
| Rows by partition and order | Wide-column | Is the partition key known in every query? |
| Large aggregates over few columns | Columnar analytic | How fresh must results be? |
| Multi-hop relationships | Graph | How deep and selective are traversals? |

## Count the lost conveniences

A specialized store may improve one access pattern while narrowing others. Many key-value designs do not offer arbitrary joins or full-table transactions. A document model may duplicate frequently changing data. A wide-column table often fixes query order in the primary key. A graph store can make traversals natural but may be less attractive for a simple high-volume point lookup. These are model constraints, not defects; they are useful when the workload matches.

Operational fit matters too. A second database requires expertise in backups, restore, access control, monitoring, upgrades, and data movement. If a new store is a derived read model, define the authoritative source and a rebuild procedure. If it is the system of record, test its failure, consistency, and transaction behavior against the product's invariants before migration.

## Compare a concrete alternative

For the order example, start with one relational schema and benchmark the known reads and writes. If customer order history becomes a hot path, a covering index or materialized read view may suffice. If the product later needs a flexible product catalog with deeply variable attributes, a document model may be worth evaluating. If daily analytics scans billions of events, a columnar warehouse can be added as a derived store without moving checkout state.

The decision should name the workload and measured limit: “This query needs a 200 ms p95 at 10,000 reads/s and cannot meet it under the current schema and indexing,” not “NoSQL scales better.” A relational database can partition and replicate; a NoSQL database can still have hot keys and costly cross-partition work.

## Design review

List the five most important reads and writes. Which require transactions or flexible queries? Which key drives placement? What is the authority if two stores disagree? What new operational work does the chosen store add?
