04.02:
A key-value store retrieves a value by a key. A document store also keeps a structured document and can index or query fields inside it. The difference affects how you model relationships, update parts of an object, and answer queries beyond a simple lookup. The same product may use both: durable documents as authority and a key-value cache for hot responses.

## Start with the object boundary

Imagine a support ticket with subject, description, status, and a few assigned labels. Reading the whole ticket by ID is a natural document operation. Comments are trickier: if a ticket can accumulate millions of comments, embedding them all in one document makes the object huge and every update contend on it. Store comments separately, perhaps keyed by ticket ID and creation time, and keep a bounded recent-comment summary on the ticket if that helps the common read.

MongoDB's guidance favors embedding when related data is read and updated together in one atomic operation, and references when related entities grow large, change independently, or are queried on their own. The same questions apply to document modeling generally. “Schemaless” does not mean there is no contract: the application still needs field types, required values, versions, and migration rules.

| Access pattern | Key-value approach | Document approach |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Get ticket by ID | Direct key lookup | Direct document lookup |
| Filter by status and assignee | Secondary index or separate key sets | Indexed document fields |
| Update one nested field | Replace or store subkeys | Partial document update if supported |
| Read large comment history | Many keys and explicit ordering | Separate comment collection preferred |

## Make updates and indexes explicit

A key-value record may be an opaque byte string to the store. That can make point reads simple and fast, but filtering by `status` requires a separate index maintained by the application or store. If the index update and value update are not atomic, a read can see stale or missing results. A document store can maintain secondary indexes on fields, but each index adds write and storage cost, and query behavior still depends on selectivity.

Document boundaries also define atomicity. If a support ticket and its embedded labels change in one document, one write may keep them together. If ticket state and comments live in separate collections or services, a single-document guarantee does not cover both. Identify which invariants must span objects. Do not assume the word “document” implies full transaction semantics across arbitrary records.

## Plan for evolution

A new field can be added to new documents while older ones lack it. Readers need defaults or a migration. A rename can be staged: write both, read new with fallback, backfill, then remove old. Indexing a newly introduced field may require scanning existing data and additional disk. Validate query plans with old and new documents, not just fresh test data.

Choose key-value when the service truly knows the key and treats the value as a unit, such as a session or cached profile. Choose document capabilities when the product needs structured field queries and bounded aggregate objects. If both are available in one database, model from the workload rather than the product category.

## Design review

What is the maximum document or value size? Which fields must be queried without the primary key? Which related records change independently? Can the store enforce the transaction that the business rule needs?

04.03:
“Columnar” and “wide-column” sound similar but describe different storage ideas. A columnar analytical database stores values of the same column together so it can scan and compress a few fields across many rows efficiently. A wide-column operational store organizes rows by a partition key and clustering order, making known partition-local reads and writes efficient. Confusing them can lead to a poor choice for both analytics and serving.

## Columnar storage for aggregation

Suppose an event table has fifty fields and a report needs only `country`, `event_type`, and `revenue` across a billion events. A column-oriented engine can read a small fraction of the stored columns, compress similar values together, and aggregate vectors of values. It is a natural fit for large scans and group-by queries. ClickHouse describes this as an OLAP-oriented layout. It does not imply that updating one individual event or serving a low-latency transaction by primary key is its strongest path.

The query workload matters more than the name. If the report filters on time and tenant, physical ordering, partitioning, and skipping metadata can reduce scanned data further. Ingestion, merge behavior, and materialized aggregates affect freshness and cost. A columnar engine still needs a plan for late events, corrections, and deletions; append-heavy analytics is easier than frequent in-place mutation.

## Wide-column storage for partition-local access

In Cassandra, a table's primary key has a partition key and optional clustering columns. The partition key determines which replica set stores the rows; clustering columns order rows within that partition. A table for a user's messages might use `user_id` as partition key and `sent_at` as clustering key, allowing a bounded recent-message scan for one user. It is not designed to scan all users' messages and group by a field absent from the key as its ordinary online path.

| Workload | Columnar analytic store | Wide-column operational store |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sum revenue over a year | Natural scan/aggregation | Often needs precomputed view |
| Fetch newest 50 messages for one user | Possible but usually not primary strength | Natural partition scan |
| Update one account balance | Usually poor fit | Requires careful key and consistency design |
| Scan three of fifty fields | Reads selected columns efficiently | Data placement follows partition key |

Wide-column models often duplicate data in tables tailored to queries. That reduces expensive joins but creates update fanout and reconciliation obligations. The partition key must spread traffic as well as bound partition size. If a celebrity user's messages all share one partition key, that partition can become a hot spot regardless of cluster size. Bucket by time or another dimension when necessary, then accept that a read may need multiple buckets.

## Choose the authority and pipeline

A product may keep transactional orders in a relational store, serve a high-volume partition-key query from a wide-column projection, and send events to a columnar warehouse. Each additional copy needs an update pipeline, lag target, replay path, and privacy deletion policy. Avoid treating a warehouse as a synchronous source of truth for checkout simply because it stores the same records.

## Design review

Does the hot query scan many rows but few fields, or fetch a bounded range inside one known partition? How are updates and late records handled? What is the largest partition and hottest key? Which store owns the authoritative business fact?

04.04:
A graph database makes relationships first-class data. It can be valuable when the primary question is a traversal: follow several kinds of edges from one entity, filter along a path, or ask how two entities are connected. It is less compelling when the workload is mostly point lookups, flat aggregates, or simple joins that a relational database already handles well.

## Ask a path-shaped question

Consider a fraud investigation system. Accounts use devices, devices use IP addresses, and payment cards are linked to accounts. An investigator asks: “Which other accounts share a device with this account, and did any of them use the same card within two hops?” Nodes represent accounts, devices, IPs, and cards; typed relationships represent `USES_DEVICE`, `USES_IP`, and `PAID_WITH`. A traversal follows only relevant edges rather than repeatedly joining several large tables to discover an unknown path.

Neo4j's property graph model has nodes, typed directed relationships, and properties on both. That makes relationship semantics visible in the query. But a graph model does not automatically make every graph query cheap. A high-degree node, such as a shared public IP, can fan out to millions of neighbors. Bound traversal depth, filter edge types and times, and inspect query plans.

| Question | Graph fit | Alternative |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One account by ID | Little special benefit | Indexed relational or key-value lookup |
| Friends of friends with filters | Often strong | Repeated joins or precomputed view |
| Total sales by region | Usually not its main strength | Relational or columnar aggregation |
| Shortest relationship path | Natural graph operation | Custom traversal over adjacency tables |

## Model edges carefully

An edge should represent a real domain relationship with direction and lifecycle. `ACCOUNT_USES_DEVICE` may need first-seen and last-seen timestamps; a device observed once years ago should not have the same meaning as an active session. Decide whether parallel edges are allowed, whether one edge is updated, and how deletion propagates. Avoid creating a generic `RELATED_TO` edge for every relationship; it makes traversals harder to filter and reason about.

Constraints still matter. Unique account IDs and device fingerprints need indexes. Authorization and privacy matter when traversals can reveal indirect connections between people. A query that begins from an authorized account may reach other accounts the caller should not see. Filter results and possibly intermediate paths according to policy.

## Count the integration cost

A graph database often starts as a derived model from transactional records. If the order system remains authoritative, event pipelines must add and remove edges when records change. Define lag, replay, and reconciliation. A stale fraud graph may miss a recent link; a stale social graph may show an unfollowed connection. If graph writes are authoritative, the team needs backup, restore, availability, and transaction behavior appropriate to that role.

Before adding a new store, try a representative relational query with indexes or a materialized adjacency table. If common queries involve variable-depth traversals and repeated relationship filtering, a graph engine may justify itself. Benchmark the actual graph shape, especially high-degree nodes, not only a neat demonstration dataset.

## Design review

What is the central multi-hop query, and how deep can it go? Which edges are high-degree? Is the graph authoritative or derived? How are edge updates, deletions, and authorization reflected in traversals?

04.05:
Partitioning divides a dataset into smaller pieces according to a key or range. Sharding commonly means placing those pieces across independent database nodes. The purpose may be faster bounded queries, manageable retention, storage capacity, or distributed write throughput. A partition scheme is only useful when the application's important operations can find and work within the right pieces.

## Choose the key from access patterns

For a multi-tenant invoice system, `tenant_id` is a plausible shard key because most reads and writes belong to one tenant. A request can route directly to that tenant's shard. A global report across all tenants becomes a fanout or analytical pipeline. If the product frequently transfers invoices between tenants in one transaction, the key may be a poor fit. Write down the common queries and transaction boundaries before choosing placement.

Time partitioning is different. A log table divided by month makes time-bounded queries and retention easier: old partitions can be detached or dropped. But a lookup by event ID without a time hint may inspect many partitions. A hash key distributes IDs evenly but destroys natural time locality. Some systems combine levels, such as tenant then month, when both dimensions matter. Every extra dimension creates more operational metadata and routing complexity.

| Strategy | Main benefit | Main drawback |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Range by time | Efficient retention and time scans | Current range can be hot |
| Hash by tenant | Spreads many tenants | Large tenant remains hot |
| Hash by object ID | Even point lookups | Cross-object queries fan out |
| Directory/map | Flexible placement | Metadata service and map consistency |

PostgreSQL describes declarative table partitioning as splitting one logical table into physical pieces, with partition pruning for queries that constrain the partition key. That is useful even on one database server, but it does not add machine-level capacity by itself. Moving partitions to different machines introduces routing, replication, migration, and cross-shard transactions.

## Plan for rebalancing before it is urgent

A key-to-shard mapping changes when nodes are added or one node grows too large. With fixed `hash(key) mod N`, changing `N` can remap much of the data. Logical partitions decouple key assignment from physical nodes: many logical shards are mapped to machines, and a subset can move at a time. Migration needs a sequence: copy existing data, capture concurrent writes, verify counts and checksums, switch routing, then retire the old copy. Reads and writes during cutover must have one authoritative owner.

Global constraints become harder. A database unique index can enforce an email address within one shard, not necessarily across all shards. A globally unique ID generator, a directory service, or a separate uniqueness authority may be needed. Multi-shard transactions add coordination or application workflows. These costs should be justified by measured limits, not by a desire for a distributed diagram.

## Measure balance as work, not record count

Two shards with equal rows can have very different traffic. A single active tenant may dominate writes and lock contention. Track per-partition bytes, reads, writes, latency, and growth. Set thresholds for split or move operations and test them before the largest tenant reaches an emergency state.

## Design review

Can every hot operation name its partition key? Which operations fan out? What happens when one tenant or time range is much hotter than others? How does a live migration preserve one authoritative writer?

04.06:
A hot partition receives much more work than its peers and reaches a per-partition limit even when the cluster has spare capacity. More nodes do not automatically help if all requests for one key still route to one partition. The fix depends on whether the hotness comes from one item, one partition key grouping many items, or a time range that concentrates current writes.

## Identify the shape of the hot spot

Imagine a live event where millions of viewers increment one `viewer_count` item. The partition holding that key sees nearly all writes. A hash function distributes *different* keys, but one key still has one hash result. In another case, `customer_id` is a partition key and one enterprise customer has far more orders than the rest. A third case is a time-ordered key where all new writes land in the latest range. Each needs a different remedy.

Measure per-key and per-partition request rate, bytes, throttles, p99 latency, and storage size. A cluster-wide average can hide a saturated shard. AWS DynamoDB guidance explicitly warns that partition keys with poor request distribution can throttle while overall capacity is underused.

| Hotness pattern | Possible response | Cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One read-heavy item | Cache or replicate reads | Invalidation and staleness |
| One write-heavy counter | Sharded counters | Merge reads and approximate freshness |
| Large tenant | Bucket within tenant | Queries merge buckets |
| Current time range | Hash suffix or time buckets | Range scans touch several pieces |

## Split work only when semantics allow it

For a view counter, write to `count#0` through `count#31` chosen by a request hash, then sum the shards for a read. This raises write capacity at the cost of a more expensive or delayed total. It works because increments commute and an approximate count is often acceptable. It is unsafe for an inventory balance if two purchases must atomically compete for the last unit; splitting that invariant needs a reservation allocation scheme, not a blind counter sum.

For a hot tenant, add a bucket key such as `(tenant_id, month)` or `(tenant_id, bucket_id)` while keeping the tenant ID available for authorization. A query for one tenant may need to merge several buckets. Design pagination and ordering across them; a simple local `LIMIT 20` on each bucket does not necessarily produce the correct global top twenty without a merge.

## Beware of adaptive fixes

Some managed stores can split partitions or adapt to hot traffic, but one indivisible item or key can remain a bottleneck. Do not rely on automatic scaling as the only hot-key plan. Caches can relieve reads but not high-rate writes to one authoritative record. More application replicas can worsen contention on the same database row.

Write sharding needs a deterministic or random bucket selection and a way to discover all buckets later. If random buckets are added during a live migration, old and new readers must agree on the bucket count. Monitor skew after the change: a small number of buckets can still be uneven, while too many buckets make reads expensive. Test at realistic key popularity distributions, not uniform synthetic traffic.

## Design review

Is the hot spot one key, one tenant, or one range? Which invariant requires a single writer? If work is split, how are reads merged and how fresh is the answer? What happens when bucket count changes?

04.07:
Consistent hashing assigns keys to a changing set of nodes while minimizing remapping when membership changes. In a storage system, it is a placement mechanism: it tells a router or coordinator which node or token range owns a key. It does not by itself replicate data, transfer bytes, ensure one writer, or make a hot key less hot.

## Compare with modulo placement

With `hash(key) mod 4`, four nodes each own some keys. Adding a fifth node changes the divisor; many existing keys now map elsewhere. If those keys hold durable data, the system must move a large fraction of the dataset before routing is correct. Consistent hashing maps keys and node positions into one circular hash space. A key belongs to the next owner clockwise. Adding a node takes a bounded interval from an existing owner, leaving most keys where they were.

The original Karger paper introduced this idea for distributed caching. For durable storage, the placement rule becomes only one part of a larger protocol. Cassandra documents a partitioned model using a variant of consistent hashing and replication across nodes. A production design also needs a consistent membership view, replica selection, handoff, repair, and failure handling.

| Property | What consistent hashing helps | What it does not solve |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Node addition | Limits remapped key range | Copies data automatically |
| Node failure | Identifies new owner/replicas | Guarantees no lost writes |
| Balance | Distributes many random keys | Splits one extremely hot key |
| Routing | Stable key-to-node rule | Keeps all routers in sync |

## Smooth imbalance with virtual positions

A few randomly placed physical nodes can own uneven arc lengths. Assigning each node many virtual positions, often called tokens or virtual nodes, reduces variance and makes it easier to distribute a node's share across the ring. Weights can give stronger machines more positions. The tradeoff is more routing metadata and potentially more transfer streams during rebalancing. Measure work distribution, not merely key counts: a node with a popular key may be overloaded despite equal token ranges.

Rendezvous hashing and jump consistent hashing are related alternatives with different implementation properties. Jump hashing is compact when buckets are numbered in a controlled sequence; a ring may be more flexible for weighted physical nodes and token ranges. Choose an algorithm whose membership and migration behavior the team can operate. The exact formula matters less than a tested handoff protocol.

## Make ownership transitions safe

When a node joins, old and new owners may temporarily disagree. A safe transition can mark a range as moving, copy a snapshot, stream later writes, verify state, and then switch the authoritative routing version. Clients or gateways must not blindly use stale maps for writes. A lease, epoch, or fencing token can prevent an old owner from accepting writes after handoff. If the store is replicated, define which replicas acknowledge during the move and how missed writes are repaired.

For a cache, a short period of misses may be acceptable; keys can be repopulated from authority. For durable data, the same loss is unacceptable. That difference should drive how much coordination the placement change requires.

## Design review

How do all routers learn the same membership version? What data moves when a node is added? Who may accept writes during handoff? How does the system detect and repair missing replicas? What happens to a single key that owns half the traffic?

04.08:
Distributed ID generation gives independent writers a way to assign unique names to records before a central database commit. The design choice affects availability, index locality, information exposed to clients, and what ordering can be inferred. Start by separating the requirements: uniqueness, size, approximate time order, unguessability, and whether an ID must be created while disconnected.

## Compare coordination with local generation

A single database sequence is simple and can produce compact integers, but every issuer depends on that database. A ticket server centralizes only ID allocation, which may be cheaper than centralizing all writes, yet still adds a network hop. Range allocation lets an application node lease a block of IDs and issue them locally; unused values are lost on crash, which is usually acceptable. UUIDs can be generated without shared coordination, with a collision probability designed to be negligible when the generator follows the specification.

Time-based IDs combine a timestamp, worker identity, and per-time-unit sequence. Twitter's Snowflake design used that composition to obtain roughly sortable 64-bit IDs without a coordinated call for every ID. It still needed unique worker numbers at startup. The distinction is subtle: the hot path can be uncoordinated while worker assignment remains coordinated.

| Requirement | Candidate approach | Hidden obligation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Compact integer | Sequence or Snowflake-style | Issuer availability or clock/worker IDs |
| Offline generation | UUID | Entropy and format handling |
| Rough time order | UUIDv7 or Snowflake-style | Clock rollback policy |
| Unpredictable public token | Random identifier | Enough entropy and abuse controls |
| Strict total order | Coordinated sequencer | Availability and throughput ceiling |

## Define the uniqueness scope

An ID may be unique per table, per tenant, per entity type, or across the entire product. Two services can safely use `42` if every reference includes entity type; they cannot if a public API accepts only one bare numeric ID for all objects. Worker identifiers must be unique among concurrently active generators. Reusing a worker ID while an old process is still alive can create collisions at the same timestamp and sequence value.

Do not confuse uniqueness with commit order. A writer can allocate ID 101, pause, while another writer allocates 102 and commits first. A client sorting by ID may then see records out of real creation order. Even a time-embedded ID is only as accurate as the generating clocks and timestamp granularity. If strict order matters, use an authoritative commit timestamp or sequence designed for that guarantee.

## Fit the identifier to storage and APIs

Random keys can scatter B-tree inserts, affecting locality; roughly increasing keys may append more predictably but can concentrate writes in a particular range or expose traffic timing. Wider IDs increase index and foreign-key storage. For JavaScript clients, a 64-bit integer may exceed exact numeric representation, so send it as a string. Do not expose an internal incremental ID if it reveals sensitive business volume or makes enumeration easy; authorization remains necessary regardless of ID format.

Test restart, clock rollback, same-millisecond bursts, worker reassignment, and sequence exhaustion. Keep a unique database constraint as a final guard where possible. The chosen generator should fail closed rather than knowingly issuing duplicates when its assumptions break.

## Design review

Which guarantees are required: uniqueness, order, compactness, or secrecy? Can two live workers share an identity? What happens when the clock moves backward or a local range is exhausted? Can a client safely handle the ID's numeric width?

04.09:
UUID, MongoDB ObjectId, and Snowflake-style IDs solve overlapping but different identifier problems. Their byte widths, time structure, and operational assumptions differ. Choose one by the guarantees your callers and storage engine actually need, then state what it does **not** promise.

## Compare the formats

A UUID is 128 bits. RFC 9562 defines several versions: version 4 uses random bits; version 7 places a millisecond Unix timestamp in the leading bits and leaves the rest for random or monotonic subfields. UUIDv7 is useful when independent generation and roughly time-ordered storage are desired. A random UUIDv4 has no embedded time order.

MongoDB ObjectId is 12 bytes: a four-byte timestamp in seconds, a five-byte process-random component, and a three-byte counter. MongoDB notes that ObjectIds are approximately ordered by creation time, but not strictly monotonic across clients or within a second. It is a convenient native document key, not an authoritative event clock.

A Snowflake-style ID is commonly a 64-bit integer composed of time, worker identity, and a local sequence. The precise bit allocation and epoch are implementation decisions. Twitter's published design emphasized compact 64-bit values and rough ordering at high issuance rates. Unique worker identity and clock behavior become part of correctness.

| Format | Typical width | Time signal | Coordination on each ID? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| UUIDv4 | 128 bits | None | No |
| UUIDv7 | 128 bits | Millisecond prefix | No, with correct generator |
| ObjectId | 96 bits | Second prefix | No per ID |
| Snowflake-style | 64 bits | Configured timestamp field | No per ID, worker IDs coordinated |

## Separate order from identity

A time-structured ID can be useful for pagination or approximate chronological display, but it does not automatically provide strict creation order. Two machines have different clocks; two IDs generated in one millisecond may be ordered by random or worker bits rather than business commit time. If a feed must be correctly ordered, store a business timestamp and a stable tie-breaker, or use a commit sequence with clear semantics.

IDs can leak information. ObjectId and UUIDv7 encode time; Snowflake-like IDs can often reveal approximate creation time and worker structure. Public APIs should not assume an opaque-looking string is secret. Authorization must protect resources even when IDs are hard to guess. If unpredictable invitation tokens are required, generate a separate cryptographically random token with sufficient entropy instead of repurposing a sortable database key.

## Consider representation and indexes

Store IDs in native binary or integer types when supported rather than verbose text if index size matters. A 64-bit integer sent to JavaScript as a JSON number can lose precision above `2^53 - 1`; serialize as a string or use a format the client handles exactly. For relational foreign keys, a 128-bit UUID uses more bytes than a 64-bit integer in every referencing index. Test the real database and workload before treating that difference as decisive.

The ID format should be stable over a long product life. Migrating primary keys across APIs, caches, logs, and foreign keys is expensive. If requirements are uncertain, a standard UUIDv7 can be a reasonable independently generated default; if compact numeric IDs are a hard requirement, invest in worker and clock operations.

## Design review

Which guarantees come from the format and which from the generator implementation? Can clients store it losslessly? Does its timestamp expose information? Would sorting by the ID produce the exact business order users expect?

04.10:
A Snowflake-style generator packs a timestamp, a worker ID, and a per-timestamp sequence into a compact integer. It allows many workers to issue IDs locally while keeping values roughly ordered by time. The design succeeds only if worker IDs never overlap while active, clocks are handled conservatively, and sequence capacity is not exceeded.

## Choose a bit budget

For illustration, reserve one sign bit, 41 bits for milliseconds since a custom epoch, 10 bits for worker identity, and 12 bits for a sequence. That permits 1,024 worker numbers and 4,096 sequence values per worker per millisecond, while 41 timestamp bits span about 69 years. These are **example limits of this layout**, not a promise that the service can sustain 4,096 durable writes per millisecond: network, storage, and downstream systems may be much slower.

The packed value is conceptually `(timestamp << 22) | (worker << 12) | sequence`. A custom epoch reduces the bits needed for dates near deployment. Document the epoch forever; changing it or the bit allocation without a version marker can make old and new IDs decode differently. Keep the sign bit clear if clients or databases use signed 64-bit integers.

| Field | Purpose | Failure to handle |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Timestamp | Rough chronological order | Clock rollback or epoch exhaustion |
| Worker ID | Disjoint issuers | Two active workers share ID |
| Sequence | Burst within one millisecond | Counter wraps before clock advances |

## Make issuance a state machine

On each request, read the current clock. If it is later than the last issued millisecond, reset the sequence. If it is equal, increment the sequence. If the sequence is exhausted, wait until the next millisecond or return a bounded error; never wrap and reuse a value. If the clock moved backward, stop issuance, wait within a configured bound, or use a carefully persisted logical time policy. Silently resetting the sequence can create duplicates when the old millisecond recurs.

Worker assignment is another state machine. A lease or coordinator can allocate unique IDs to live workers. A new worker should not reuse an ID until the old holder is fenced and the maximum relevant time window is safe. Container restarts and network partitions make “machine number in config” risky if two instances can boot with the same value. Monitor lease renewal and fail closed on uncertainty.

## Define the order promise honestly

IDs generated by one worker with a nondecreasing clock can be monotonic. Across workers, clocks differ and sequence fields overlap, so the numeric order is only approximate. A write can allocate an ID and commit later than a record with a larger ID. Twitter's announcement described its IDs as roughly sortable rather than globally sorted. Use a separate commit-order mechanism when the product requires exact ordering.

Test the generator under frozen time, backward time, many threads, worker-ID collision, and restart. Verify uniqueness with a database constraint in an integration workload. Estimate the date when the timestamp field overflows and establish a migration strategy well before it arrives.

## Design review

What is the layout and epoch? How does the worker ID remain unique through restart and partition? What does the generator do on clock rollback and sequence exhaustion? Can every client represent the resulting integer exactly?

04.11:
Clock skew means two machines disagree about wall time, or one machine's clock jumps. It matters for time-embedded IDs, TTLs, leases, event order, and “latest” queries. An ID with a timestamp prefix is not a substitute for a globally agreed commit order. Design each use of time around the accuracy it actually needs.

## See how a clock creates an ID bug

Suppose a Snowflake-style worker issued IDs at millisecond 5000 with sequences 0 through 50. Its clock is corrected backward to 4999 and later returns to 5000. If the generator reset its sequence when time changed, it can issue `(5000, worker, 0)` again. A unique constraint may catch the duplicate, but the generator has violated its contract. It should detect backward movement before resetting state, then wait, fail, or use a documented logical-time mechanism.

UUIDv7 also embeds millisecond time. RFC 9562 discusses monotonic counters and clock rollback handling. A generator can preserve per-process monotonic order by retaining the last timestamp and incrementing a counter, but persistence across restarts and behavior across nodes need separate thought. Random bits protect uniqueness probabilistically; they do not make the timestamp accurate.

| Use of time | Risk from skew | Better contract |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sort user posts | Misordered posts | Timestamp plus stable tie-breaker, accept bounded disorder |
| Lease expiry | Old owner acts after lease | Fencing token checked by resource |
| TTL | Premature or late expiration | Authority uses one clock and clear semantics |
| Audit sequence | Wrong causality inference | Commit order or logical sequence |

## Distinguish wall time from logical order

Wall-clock timestamps answer approximate “when.” A monotonically increasing local counter answers “which came next on this process.” Lamport clocks or database commit sequences can represent causal or authoritative order under specific rules, but neither is the same as a precise wall-clock time. If a payment record needs a defensible order of commits, define it at the ledger's commit point rather than sorting application-server timestamps.

For distributed transactions, systems that require external consistency invest in stronger clock and coordination mechanisms. Google Spanner's TrueTime API reports time uncertainty and uses it in its ordering guarantee. That is more than synchronizing clocks with a standard time daemon; it is an architectural commitment with latency and operational consequences. Most applications should avoid promising global real-time order unless the product truly requires it.

## Make uncertainty visible

Monitor clock offset and synchronization status on ID-generating nodes. Alert before offset approaches the maximum tolerated skew. Log both event time and server receipt or commit time when debugging pipelines. For delayed messages, distinguish “the event occurred at” from “the broker accepted it at” and “the consumer processed it at.” A late event can have an earlier business timestamp without being a duplicate.

If pagination sorts by `(created_at, id)`, the pair gives stable ties but not necessarily causal order across servers. New late-arriving rows may appear before a cursor the user has passed. Decide whether the feed prioritizes exact snapshot traversal, approximate freshness, or a bounded delay window.

## Design review

Which machine's clock assigns the timestamp? How large can skew be before correctness breaks? Is the required order per worker, per entity, or global? What happens after a clock correction or restart?

04.12:
Pagination divides a changing result set into manageable responses. Offset pagination names a position in the current result, while keyset pagination names the last item actually seen. That difference matters when a list is large or new rows arrive between requests. Choose the contract before choosing the SQL: a live feed, a stable export, and a numbered catalog need different behavior.

## See why an offset moves

Imagine posts ordered newest first. Page one returns positions 1 through 20. A new post arrives before the reader requests `OFFSET 20 LIMIT 20`; the old position 20 is now position 21, so it appears again. A deletion can cause a row to be skipped. A unique `ORDER BY` makes each individual query deterministic, but it does not freeze the result across requests. PostgreSQL also notes that skipped offset rows still need to be computed, making deep pages expensive.

Offset is fine for small administrative tables or interfaces where direct page numbers are valuable and moderate churn is acceptable. It is a poor default for an endless feed with millions of rows. Do not promise stable traversal from offset alone.

## Seek after the last key

For a descending feed ordered by creation time and unique ID, return a cursor containing the last row's two values. The next request seeks below that pair:

```sql
SELECT id, created_at, title
FROM posts
WHERE tenant_id = $1
  AND (created_at, id) < ($2, $3)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 21;
```

With a page size of 20, the extra row tells the API whether another page exists. A supporting index might begin with `tenant_id`, then `(created_at DESC, id DESC)`. The unique ID breaks timestamp ties; without it, rows sharing the boundary timestamp can be missed or repeated. PostgreSQL's row comparison evaluates the pair lexicographically, matching this ordering when both keys descend. Null sort keys need an explicit policy because ordinary row comparisons involving null can yield unknown.

Keep the cursor opaque to clients, but document its meaning. Encode a version, sort values, and any fixed filter or tenant scope. Validate decoded values and apply authorization on every page. A signature can prevent clients from forging expensive or cross-scope cursors, but it does not replace server-side authorization. A cursor tied to a different filter should be rejected rather than quietly returning surprising rows.

## Define consistency across pages

Keyset pagination avoids shifting offsets and makes indexed deep traversal practical. It does not provide a snapshot by itself. A row inserted with a newer key after page one will be above the cursor and will not appear later in that traversal. A late-arriving row with an older key may appear later. An updated sort key can move a row across the boundary. For an audit export requiring exact coverage, use a consistent snapshot or a bounded high-water mark, then document how updates and deletions are handled.

Reverse navigation needs the inverse predicate and ordering before reversing the returned page for display. Arbitrary jump-to-page is not native to a keyset cursor. If product requirements demand it, consider a separate approximate position index or bounded offset rather than pretending cursors have page numbers. Treat cursor lifetime as part of the API: old cursors may be invalid after sort changes, retention cleanup, or index migrations.

## Design review

Is the list a live feed or a stable report? Does the ordering contain a unique tie-breaker? Which index supports both the filter and seek? What should happen if a cursor is stale, modified, or used with different filters?

04.13:
A Bloom filter is a compact test for possible membership. It can say “definitely absent” or “possibly present” when its construction and updates are correct. The second answer is deliberately uncertain: some absent keys are false positives. This makes Bloom filters useful before an expensive exact lookup, but unsuitable as the only source of truth for a decision that requires proof of presence.

## Build the membership sketch

Start with an array of `m` zero bits and choose `k` hash positions for each key. Insertion sets those positions to one. A lookup returns absent if any position is zero; otherwise it returns possibly present. One key can set bits later reused by other keys. As the filter fills, more absent keys happen to find all their positions set, so false positives rise. An intact, correctly updated filter has no false negatives for inserted keys because insertion only sets bits.

The usual approximate false-positive probability after `n` insertions is `(1 - exp(-kn/m))^k`. This is a planning model, not a service-level guarantee under every workload or hash implementation. Reserve enough bits for expected cardinality and choose the hash count for the target rate. Estimate growth over the filter's lifetime, including retries and duplicate insertions. If the dataset exceeds planned capacity, measure the actual rate and rebuild or scale the filter rather than assuming its original sizing still applies.

## Put it in front of an exact store

Suppose a service checks whether an object key exists in a remote database. A local Bloom filter can reject most random misses without a network call. A “possibly present” response still goes to the database. The benefit depends on the miss fraction, filter size, false-positive rate, and cost of the exact lookup. If almost every query is a hit, the filter adds memory and CPU while saving little. If the filter is on a separate network service, that extra hop may erase the gain.

The filter's update path is the difficult part. If a write commits to the database but the filter misses the insertion, the filter can incorrectly reject a real key. Build it from a trusted snapshot and replay writes from a durable change stream, or fail open to the exact store while freshness is uncertain. Version each filter build and atomically replace it only after catch-up. A negative filter result should never deny a user access to data unless the system can prove the filter is current and the decision tolerates its failure modes.

## Handle deletion and lifecycle

Clearing an ordinary Bloom-filter bit on deletion is unsafe: another key may rely on that bit and become a false negative. Counting Bloom filters store small counters so deletions can decrement the positions, but counters add space and require careful handling of duplicates and overflow. Simpler systems leave bits set and periodically rebuild; deleted keys then remain possible false positives until the rebuild.

Place the filter near the workload that benefits from it and decide what happens on process restart. A stale or unavailable filter should usually cause extra exact lookups, not missing data. Monitor filter fill ratio, estimated false-positive rate, rebuild lag, and exact-store requests avoided. Test the negative path against known inserted keys after recovery and replays.

## Design review

What fraction of lookups are absent? Can the filter be updated after every committed write? What is the safe fallback when freshness is unknown? How are deletions, capacity growth, and rebuilds handled?

04.14:
Hot and cold storage describe access expectations, not merely two price tags. Hot data is read or changed frequently and needs low latency. Cold data is rarely accessed but still has retention, recovery, privacy, and deletion obligations. Archival moves data through those expectations over time. A useful design specifies the retrieval experience and the full lifecycle before choosing a storage class.

## Separate data from its access path

Consider customer statements. The latest statements might be fetched directly from object storage through an application API. Older statements could move to an archival class while metadata such as customer ID, document date, checksum, retention deadline, and storage location stays queryable in the primary database. That metadata lets the application list old statements without restoring every document. The bytes and metadata must remain consistent: if a lifecycle transition or delete occurs, an old database pointer should not silently produce a broken download.

Storage tiers differ in retrieval delay, per-request charges, minimum storage duration, and operational constraints. Amazon S3, for example, offers multiple storage classes with different access patterns and archival retrieval behavior. A lower per-gigabyte rate can cost more overall when users retrieve frequently, objects are small, or data is deleted before a minimum duration. Model monthly storage, transitions, retrievals, requests, and the staff cost of handling delayed reads.

## Design the restore workflow

If a cold object cannot be read immediately, the API should return a clear pending state instead of holding a web request open for an unknown duration. Persist a restore job with a stable ID; deduplicate repeat requests; notify the user when ready; and give the temporary restored copy an expiry. Make the download endpoint check authorization again when the restore completes. A user who could request a restore yesterday may have lost access today.

An archive may be a backup source, but archival storage alone is not a recovery plan. Decide how quickly the business must restore a single object, a tenant, and the whole dataset. Exercise bulk recovery, including metadata reconstruction, encryption keys, and regional failure assumptions. An index that points to cold bytes must be recoverable too.

## Apply lifecycle and deletion rules

Automated lifecycle rules can transition or expire objects by age or other criteria. The transition schedule should begin from a product requirement such as “full-speed access for 90 days,” then be tested against real access data. AWS documents eligibility and minimum-duration considerations for transitions; validate them for the chosen classes before forecasting savings. Versioned objects, multipart uploads, and failed transitions can complicate the bill and deletion process.

Retention and privacy rules may pull in opposite directions. A legal hold can prohibit deletion while a user deletion request may require it when no hold applies. Keep a record of the governing policy and make deletion cover primary copies, archive copies, versions, caches, and search indexes. Encryption helps protect stored bytes, but losing a key is not a substitute for a documented deletion workflow. Produce an audit trail that records what was transitioned, restored, expired, and deleted.

## Design review

How often are old objects actually retrieved? What latency is acceptable for a restore? Where does searchable metadata live? How are authorization, retention, and deletion enforced across all copies? Does the cost model include retrieval and minimum-duration charges?

05.01:
A cache stores a copy of data closer to a reader or in a form that is cheaper to serve. “Closer” may mean a browser, CDN, application process, distributed memory service, or precomputed database view. Each layer has a different owner, scope, latency, and invalidation path. Start with the slow read and its freshness requirement, then choose the narrowest layer that fixes it.

## Place copies along the request path

A public product image can be cached by a browser and CDN because many users request identical bytes. A personalized account balance may belong only in a short-lived application cache, or may be uncached if stale data would mislead the user. A database buffer pool already caches disk pages; adding Redis in front of a query that is fast and rare may only add a network hop and an outage mode.

| Layer | Good fit | Main constraint |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Browser | Static assets, safe private responses | User controls the copy and its lifetime |
| CDN or shared HTTP cache | Public, reusable responses | Cache key and privacy must be correct |
| Process memory | Tiny, frequently reused local state | Each process has a separate view |
| Distributed cache | Shared high-volume reads | Network, capacity, and invalidation cost |
| Materialized view | Repeated expensive aggregation | Refresh lag and write maintenance |

The request path may contain several layers. On a miss, each layer passes to the next until the authoritative store answers. Measure latency by hit and miss separately. An overall average can hide a small number of very slow misses or cache warmups.

## Match the copy to its identity

An HTTP cache key usually begins with the request target and relevant request headers, but applications often have hidden dimensions: tenant, language, authorization, feature flag, or output format. Accidentally sharing a personalized response is a data leak, not merely a stale result. RFC 9111 defines the semantics of shared and private HTTP caches, freshness, and validation. Use explicit cache controls, vary responses only on intended dimensions, and test authenticated requests through every intermediary.

Inside an application, a cache key should encode the data identity and the representation version. For example, `tenant:42:product:91:v3` prevents one tenant's data from colliding with another's and allows a schema transition without misreading old serialized values. Do not rely on a TTL to correct a broken key design. Keep high-cardinality variants in mind: caching every unique search query can fill memory while producing few hits.

## Decide how each layer becomes fresh

TTL bounds how long a copy can remain without renewal, but it is not an exact invalidation guarantee. A write can invalidate a cache entry, update it, or let it age out. Event-driven invalidation adds delivery and ordering problems. HTTP validators such as ETag can revalidate a stored response without transferring its full body when unchanged. The right approach depends on how stale the product can be and how often the source changes.

Work from a quantitative example. If a read endpoint receives 10,000 requests per second and the database can safely handle 1,000, a 95% cache hit rate leaves about 500 requests per second at the database. But a cold start or outage can suddenly send all 10,000 there. Capacity and fallback must account for the miss path, not just steady-state savings.

## Design review

Which requests share an identical answer? Where is the authoritative copy? What freshness error can users tolerate? How do keys include tenant and representation scope? Can the source survive a cold cache?

05.02:
A distributed cache gives many application instances a shared, fast copy of data. It helps when process-local caches duplicate too much memory or diverge too easily. It also becomes a service on the critical read path. Design it around key distribution, source-of-truth semantics, capacity, and failure behavior before choosing a cluster size.

## Choose a read and write pattern

With cache-aside, an application reads the cache, fetches the database on a miss, and then fills the cache. Writes usually update the database and invalidate the corresponding cache entry. This keeps the database authoritative and makes misses easy to reason about, but concurrent misses can stampede it. Write-through populates the cache when a write happens, which can make the next read fast, at the cost of caching data that may never be read. AWS describes the two patterns as complementary rather than universal alternatives.

Be precise about failure between database commit and invalidation. If a write commits but the cache deletion fails, readers may see the old value until expiry. A short TTL can bound staleness, but only if the product accepts that bound. A durable outbox event can improve retryability. For strict read-after-write behavior, route the writer's next read to the source or carry a version; do not claim that asynchronous invalidation is immediately consistent.

## Partition keys without losing semantics

A single cache node eventually reaches a memory, network, or CPU limit. Sharding maps keys to nodes. Redis Cluster uses 16,384 hash slots and assigns ranges of slots to masters; clients follow the slot map during normal use and migration. This is a concrete alternative to client-side consistent hashing. Multi-key operations require compatible placement, so a key naming scheme can become part of the data model. A hot key remains hot even when the rest of the keyspace is evenly distributed.

Replicas can improve availability or read scale, but they may lag the primary. Decide whether a replica read can return an older version. Failover may lose recent cache writes, which is usually acceptable for a rebuildable cache but not for authoritative state. If the cache holds sessions, locks, or counters that cannot be reconstructed, it has stopped being “just a cache” and needs stronger durability analysis.

## Keep the working set affordable

Estimate memory from serialized value bytes, key bytes, per-entry overhead, replication factor, and allocator headroom. A million 1 KB values is more than one gigabyte in practice. Set a capacity limit and choose an eviction policy based on expected access. If entries are needed for correctness, eviction is not safe. For ordinary cached copies, watch hit rate, evictions, fragmentation, network saturation, and p95/p99 latency by node and tenant.

Use bounded request timeouts and connection pools. A slow cache can be worse than a failed cache because every application worker waits. Before rollout, load-test a cold cluster and a node migration. Warm a small set of genuinely hot keys if necessary, but avoid indiscriminately loading the entire database into memory. Plan how a new serialization version rolls through old cache entries.

## Design review

Can every cached value be reconstructed? What happens after a committed write and failed invalidation? Which keys are hot, and can one shard absorb them? What is the source load if the cluster is empty or unavailable?

05.03:
Eviction chooses which entries leave a full cache so new entries can enter. It is a memory-pressure policy, distinct from expiration, which makes an entry ineligible after a time or deadline. A cache can have TTLs but no evictions, evictions but no TTLs, or both. Choose eviction from the workload's reuse pattern and measure its effect on the authoritative store.

## Compare the common policies

Least recently used (LRU) favors keys touched recently. It works well when recent access predicts the next request, but a one-time scan can push useful older entries out. Least frequently used (LFU) favors repeatedly accessed keys, making it more resistant to scans, but a historical winner can remain after demand shifts unless frequency decays. FIFO is simpler and cheap, but age alone may have little connection to value. Random eviction can be surprisingly competitive under some workloads and is easy to implement, yet it offers little protection for a very hot item.

An ideal policy also accounts for value size and refill cost. A 10 MB object used once may evict thousands of tiny, popular keys. A cache for expensive reports may need an admission rule that refuses one-off results and admits only keys observed more than once. This is different from eviction: admission asks whether a new item should enter at all, while eviction asks which resident item should leave.

| Policy | Tends to preserve | Common weakness |
| --- | --- | --- |
| LRU | Recent working set | Sequential scans can pollute it |
| LFU | Long-lived hot set | Needs aging when popularity shifts |
| FIFO | Newest arrivals | Ignores actual reuse |
| No eviction | Every stored key until expiry or delete | New writes fail at capacity |

## Read the implementation's real contract

Redis documents `allkeys` and `volatile` eviction families. A volatile policy considers only keys with an expiry; persistent keys are not candidates. If the application forgets to set TTLs, the eligible pool may be too small and writes can fail. Redis's LRU is sampled and approximate rather than a perfect global ordering; its LFU uses probabilistic frequency estimation and decay. These details matter when diagnosing misses, though an application should usually select by measured behavior rather than fine-tuning the algorithm first.

Set the memory ceiling with space for replication, persistence, client buffers, and operational overhead. “Maximum cache data memory” is not necessarily “maximum process RSS.” Test what the client sees when no key can be evicted. A failed cache write should not silently turn a successful database write into a user-visible failure unless cache population is part of the explicit contract.

## Evaluate with workload traces

Hit rate alone is incomplete. A cache that hits many cheap tiny requests but misses the expensive queries may save little database work. Track byte hit rate, source queries avoided, refill latency, evictions by reason, and top hot keys. Replay representative request traces through candidate policies, including a product launch, a batch scan, and a popularity shift. Ensure TTL and admission settings remain comparable so policy changes are measured fairly.

At high occupancy, check whether the cache churns: items are admitted, evicted, and refetched before their second use. That is a sign to improve admission, resize the cache, or change what is cached. Merely lengthening TTL may increase stale responses without solving the working-set mismatch.

## Design review

Are recent or frequent accesses more predictive for this workload? Are large or costly values weighted appropriately? Which keys are eligible for eviction? What happens when the cache cannot accept a new entry?

05.04:
A TTL says when a cached entry stops being usable. It is a freshness boundary, not a promise that the bytes disappear at that exact instant. A cache may check expiry when a key is read, remove expired entries in background work, or do both. Design the application's correctness around the read-time rule; treat physical cleanup as resource management.

## Pick a TTL from the product contract

If prices may be stale for at most one minute, a 60-second TTL is an upper bound only if entries are created from a current source and the cache never resets TTL on every read. Sliding expiration can keep a popular stale value alive indefinitely unless there is also an absolute deadline. If prices must change immediately after a write, use explicit invalidation or version-aware reads; merely reducing TTL to one second may overwhelm the database while still allowing a one-second stale window.

Different data merits different TTLs. Public content can often live longer than inventory or account state. A “not found” sentinel should usually expire faster than a positive result so a newly created record becomes visible. Add limited random jitter to independently expiring keys when many values are populated together. This spreads refills and cleanup work instead of creating a synchronized spike.

## Separate logical expiry from reaping

Redis supports key expiration and records an expiry time that continues to advance across a server restart. A key can be found expired when accessed, and background work can also remove expired keys. The application should see an expired key as a miss even if its allocation has not yet been reclaimed. Do not assume an expiry callback fires at the exact TTL boundary or use cache reaping as the sole scheduler for billing, legal deletion, or other required actions.

An application-owned cache reaper may scan entries, delete those past deadline, and free memory in batches. Its scan rate trades CPU for memory. A full synchronous sweep can create latency spikes; incremental cleanup smooths work but leaves expired allocations longer. If a service handles millions of keys, measure the ratio of expired-but-resident bytes, sweep duration, and allocation pressure. Include expiry metadata in memory estimates.

## Avoid expiry-driven load spikes

A hot key expiring can send many readers to the source simultaneously. Jitter helps when many independent keys share a TTL, but it does not solve a single hot key. Use per-key single-flight loading, refresh before expiry, or bounded stale serving where the product permits it. A soft expiry can trigger a background refresh while a hard expiry stops serving the old value. Document both ages clearly; otherwise “five-minute TTL” can accidentally mean much longer stale exposure.

If refresh fails, decide whether to serve stale data, return an error, or query a different source. For an informational catalog, stale-if-error may be reasonable for a short bound. For a security entitlement, old data may be unacceptable. HTTP caching has explicit freshness and stale-response semantics; use those when an HTTP intermediary is part of the path rather than inventing ambiguous headers.

## Design review

What is the maximum permitted age of a response? Does any read extend that age? What happens when many keys expire together? Are cleanup and business deletion separate? Can stale data be served during source failure, and for how long?

05.05:
Cache concurrency appears when several readers miss the same key, or a write races with a refill. The cache can remain internally consistent while still serving an old business value. Design concurrency around the authoritative version and the exact order in which a value may enter the cache.

## Collapse simultaneous misses

Suppose a popular key expires and 500 requests arrive while its database query takes 100 milliseconds. Without coordination, all 500 may issue the same query. Single-flight loading lets one request fetch and the others wait briefly for the result. Within one process, a map of in-flight promises can be enough. Across processes, a short-lived lock or lease can coordinate, but the lock itself adds failure modes. The Redis cache-aside examples use a per-key token and atomic acquisition; release checks the token so an old owner cannot delete a newer owner's lock.

Waiters need a deadline and a fallback. A loader can crash, time out, or finish after its lease expires. After waiting, re-read the cache; if it is still empty, allow a bounded number of source reads or return a controlled error. Do not let all waiting requests spin forever. Limit concurrent refills globally as well as per key, since thousands of different cold keys can overload the database even with perfect single-flight for each one.

## Prevent stale refill after a write

Consider this order: reader A misses; A begins a slow database read and sees version 4; writer B commits version 5 and deletes the cache key; A then stores version 4 in the cache. Invalidation happened correctly, yet the cache now contains an old value until expiry. A common defense is to store a version or update timestamp with the value and conditionally replace only if the incoming version is at least the cached version. This still needs a way to know that version 5 exists after its invalidation; a per-key generation token or write-through update can supply it.

For strict read-after-write behavior, the writer can bypass the cache for its own subsequent reads, or the service can require a minimum version from the caller. If stale reads are acceptable, a short TTL and invalidation retry may be the simpler choice. State the tolerance explicitly instead of claiming that cache-aside is strongly consistent.

## Use locks only for the job they solve

A cache-fill lock protects the source from duplicate work. It is not automatically a safe distributed mutex for irreversible side effects. Time-limited locks can expire while a worker is paused; a second worker may acquire the same lock. If the protected resource must reject an old worker, use a monotonically increasing fencing token checked at the resource, or keep the operation in a transactional authority. Redis documents lock algorithms and their assumptions; choose the guarantee the operation actually needs.

Avoid locking the whole cache for unrelated keys. Use a per-key scope and short timeouts, and test the abandoned-lock path. Observe suppressed duplicate loads, lock wait time, source load, failed refills, and the age/version of values served. These metrics reveal whether a concurrency mechanism improves latency or merely shifts contention.

## Design review

How many readers can miss one key together? What if the loader dies or finishes after its lease? Can an old refill overwrite a newer write? Is the lock protecting refill cost or a correctness-critical side effect?

05.06:
A cache makes normal reads cheaper, but its failure can put the entire original workload back on the database. “Fall back to the database” is therefore a capacity decision, not a harmless line of exception handling. Decide which requests remain available, which can use bounded stale data, and which must be rejected when cache capacity disappears.

## Model the cold-cache load

Suppose an endpoint gets 20,000 reads per second with a 98% hit rate. The database sees roughly 400 reads per second in steady state. If the cache fails and every request goes to the database, demand becomes 50 times higher. A database sized for 1,000 reads per second cannot absorb it. The fallback needs a rate limit, admission policy, or reduced feature set. Load-test this mode before relying on it.

Even partial cache failure matters. A lost shard can send all keys in its range to the source, while healthy shards still appear fine in an aggregate hit-rate chart. Monitor hit rate and source load by shard, route, and tenant. A latency spike may indicate a slow cache rather than an outright outage; short cache timeouts and a circuit breaker keep request workers from waiting behind a failing node.

## Define degraded responses

For a public profile, a recently stored local copy might be acceptable for a short stale window. For an account balance, returning a stale value without labeling it may be worse than an error. For permissions, stale allow decisions may create a security issue. Classify endpoints by freshness and consequence, then choose one of four actions: use an authoritative source within a safe rate, serve bounded stale data, return a reduced response, or fail clearly.

A process-local emergency cache can soften a distributed-cache outage, but it is fragmented across instances and may carry older values. Make its expiry and scope explicit. Do not use a local cache to hide an invalidation bug. If an API serves stale data, expose its age or a clear stale marker where that helps callers make decisions.

## Recover without causing a second incident

When the cache returns, every node may rush to refill. Limit concurrent fills, jitter TTLs, and warm only truly hot keys. A restored cluster may have changed ownership or lost writes during failover; rebuildable copies should be reloaded from the authority. Redis Cluster can continue through some node failures but becomes unavailable under larger failures, so clients must handle both redirects and loss of service. Replicas improve cache availability but do not make cache contents authoritative.

Keep the source path healthy in ordinary operation. If the application only ever reads through the cache, a broken database connection may remain unnoticed until cache failure. Run controlled cache-bypass probes and rehearse failover. Record the database's safe read budget, cache timeout, fallback rate cap, and recovery procedure in the service runbook.

## Design review

What is the database load at zero cache hit rate? Which endpoints may serve stale data? How are fallback requests capped fairly across tenants? Can the system recover and warm the cache without overwhelming the source?

06.01:
A distributed system is a set of processes that cooperate through messages while each has only a partial view of the world. A process can fail, a message can be delayed or duplicated, and a reply can disappear after the requested action succeeded. These ordinary events create the central design problem: a caller cannot always tell whether remote work happened. Start by naming the operation's required outcome and the failures it must tolerate.

## Replace local assumptions with explicit messages

Inside one process, a function call returns or throws under one memory model. Across a network, a request may time out even though the server committed the write. Retrying a payment creation can then create a second payment unless the operation has an idempotency key or a naturally unique business identity. Acknowledgements need a precise meaning: received in memory, persisted on one node, replicated to a quorum, or applied by a downstream service are different milestones.

The same ambiguity affects reads. A replica can answer quickly with an older value. A client may have written to one region and read from another before replication catches up. The system should state which order or freshness it promises rather than using “distributed” as an explanation for surprising results.

## Plan for independent failures

A useful failure inventory includes process crash, host loss, network partition, asymmetric connectivity, disk failure, slow dependency, clock skew, and operator error. Retries help with some transient faults but can amplify load or duplicate side effects. Timeouts bound how long a caller waits; they do not cancel work that already reached the server. A circuit breaker can reduce repeated calls to a sick dependency, but it changes availability and recovery timing.

Use failure domains deliberately. Three replicas in one rack do not protect against that rack's power loss. Three replicas spread across regions may survive a regional failure but incur greater write latency and network cost. Define a recovery point objective and recovery time objective for the data and workflow before selecting the topology.

## Give every operation an authority

For each important fact, identify the component allowed to commit it. A database row can be the authority for an order's status; an event stream may distribute that status to search or analytics projections. If two services can independently finalize the same order, conflict resolution becomes part of the business rule. A replicated state machine uses an agreed log order so replicas apply commands consistently; Raft is one way to coordinate that order under its assumptions.

Avoid distributed coordination when the invariant can stay within one transactional boundary. A workflow can often use a single owner for a record plus asynchronous events for secondary views. When cross-service atomicity is unavoidable, define compensation, pending states, or a durable coordinator explicitly. The goal is not to eliminate every temporary disagreement; it is to keep the product's invariants true despite it.

## Observe the system as a chain

Trace a request across hops with a stable operation ID. Record attempt number, authoritative commit ID, queue offset, and outcome. Metrics should expose dependency latency, timeout rate, retry amplification, replication lag, and the number of operations stuck in an intermediate state. Test by delaying and dropping messages, restarting nodes, and repeating commands after lost acknowledgements. The recovery behavior is part of the design, not an appendix.

## Design review

What does success mean for this operation? Which failures can happen after a commit but before a reply? Who owns each invariant? How is a duplicate request recognized? What must remain available during a partition?

06.02:
A consistency model states which outcomes a client may observe when operations overlap or complete at different times. It is a contract over histories, not a synonym for “all replicas have identical bytes right now.” Define it for the operation and scope the product needs: one key, a transaction, one user's session, or an entire database.

## Compare observable guarantees

Linearizability makes each operation appear to take effect at a single point between its invocation and response, respecting real-time order. If a write finishes before a read starts, that read must see the write or a later one. Sequential consistency preserves each process's program order but need not preserve real-time order across processes. Eventual consistency says replicas converge if updates stop; it does not, by itself, promise when a read will catch up or how concurrent writes are resolved.

Database serializability is about transactions behaving like some serial order. It is not automatically a real-time guarantee. Strict serializability adds real-time ordering to serializable transactions. These distinctions matter when an application combines several reads and writes. A single-key linearizable register does not make a multi-key transfer atomic, and a serializable database transaction can still interact with external services in an unsafe order.

| User expectation | Useful guarantee to investigate |
| --- | --- |
| Read your own profile edit immediately | Read-your-writes for that session |
| Never display a balance older than a completed transfer | Real-time ordering at the ledger authority |
| Show all feed items eventually | Convergence plus a defined delay budget |
| Move funds between accounts atomically | Transaction isolation and durability |

## Design for the actual reader

A system may offer strong reads from a leader and faster, potentially stale reads from replicas. Let the API choose based on the operation, not on an undocumented default. An editor might route its immediate follow-up read to the leader or carry a version token until a replica catches up. A public feed can tolerate lag if users understand that posts appear after a delay. For a feature that depends on monotonic reads, stick a session to a replica that has reached its last observed version or carry the minimum version between requests.

Staleness should be measured in a useful unit: seconds behind, log entries behind, or minimum accepted version. “Eventually” is too vague for an operational objective. Even systems with strong storage semantics can present stale results through application caches, asynchronous materialized views, and CDN responses, so the end-to-end contract must include those layers.

## Test histories, not labels

Write small concurrent examples: a completed write followed by a read, two clients racing to update one value, and a transaction spanning two records. Capture invocation and completion times, returned versions, and errors during network faults. Jepsen's consistency-model reference explains these guarantees in terms of allowed histories. A database marketing label is insufficient evidence that a particular API path, transaction mode, and cache configuration obeys the required model.

If a request times out, record the outcome as unknown until the authority resolves it. A client retry with the same idempotency key can discover or safely complete the operation. Treat unknown separately from failed; that distinction avoids violating a consistency promise through a user interface that says “nothing happened” when the write may have committed.

## Design review

Which operation needs real-time ordering, and at what scope? Can a session read an older version than it already saw? What lag is acceptable for replicas and projections? How will concurrent and timed-out histories be tested?

06.03:
Replication keeps copies of data on more than one node. It can improve survival after a node failure, place reads nearer users, and sometimes spread read traffic. It also creates the question of when a write is safe to acknowledge and what a reader may see on another replica. State those semantics before drawing arrows between servers.

## Choose the write acknowledgement point

With asynchronous replication, a leader can acknowledge after a local commit and send the change later. This keeps write latency low, but a leader failure before a follower receives the change may lose an acknowledged write. Synchronous replication waits for other nodes before acknowledgement, improving durability against a single-node loss at the cost of latency and potentially availability. A quorum design commits when enough replicas confirm, assuming the quorum and failure model are correctly configured.

“Replicated” is not the same as “durable.” A follower may have received a write only in memory. A region-wide incident can remove copies that were placed in the same failure domain. Define whether acknowledgement means written to a durable log, applied to an index, or visible for reads. For every topology, test the time window between these milestones.

## Understand leader and multi-leader patterns

A single leader orders writes for its shard and simplifies conflict handling. Followers can answer stale reads unless the client waits for a known applied position or reads from the leader. Leader failover must avoid two active leaders accepting conflicting writes. Consensus-backed logs such as Raft use terms and majority agreement to choose a leader and commit an ordered sequence, but availability still requires a reachable majority.

Multi-leader or leaderless systems can accept writes in more places. Dynamo's design emphasizes high availability for a key-value workload and includes mechanisms for divergent versions and later reconciliation. That choice makes conflict semantics visible to the data model. Last-write-wins is simple but can discard an update when clocks differ or concurrent users write. A shopping cart can merge sets or preserve siblings; a bank ledger needs stronger ordering. The conflict policy is a product rule.

## Plan for lag, repair, and reads

Replication is a continuous pipeline. Monitor the distance between primary commit and replica apply, not just whether connections are up. A replica can be healthy but minutes behind after a large import or slow disk. Reads from it may violate read-your-writes. During catch-up, keep source logs long enough that a lagging replica can recover; otherwise it may need a full snapshot. Background repair and anti-entropy can fix missed updates in eventually consistent systems, but they consume bandwidth and need a way to identify divergent versions.

Place replicas across failure domains according to the incident you need to survive. Replication does not replace backup: an accidental delete or corrupted update can replicate faithfully to every node. Keep point-in-time recovery or immutable backups with tested restore procedures. A read replica also does not automatically help when the leader's write path is the bottleneck.

## Design review

When is a write acknowledged? Which replica serves a read after the client just wrote? How is a new leader chosen, and can acknowledged data be lost? What repairs divergence? Which failures do backups cover that replicas do not?
